STATEMENT AS TO WHEREABOUTS OF SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the whereabouts of the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) has been the subject of some comment both on and off the printed record in this house in the last couple of days. I am happy to assure hon. members that the minister's absence has in no way reduced the effectiveness of his department. Indeed, with the assistance of the agencies for which the Solicitor General is responsible I am pleased to report that I have tracked him down, and I find that a day or two ago in Houston, Texas, he delivered a major speech to the North American Judges Association.
Because of the very great interest of the members of this house in what the Solicitor General is doing I could read the speech he 29180-190i
made on the basis of the time taken to deliver it, which was 45 minutes. Alternatively, the speech could be found in the minister's office.

maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO WHEREABOUTS OF SOLICITOR GENERAL

In past years, Japan's restraint levels have been increased by a modest amount to permit orderly expansion of Japan's exports to Canada. Early this year, in consulting with the Canadian producers concerned, as we do each year, the government was informed that Canadian textile markets were seriously depressed. Investigations established that many sectors of the Canadian textile and garment industries are indeed experiencing difficult times. I am glad to be able to say that the Japanese government, recognizing these difficulties, has agreed to increases for 1968 that are, generally speaking, smaller than has been the case in recent years.
I should add that there have also been discussions with the Japanese authorities regarding the level of their exports to Canada of polyester/cotton fabrics. As honourable members will see, these fabrics are not included in the list of products subject to specific levels of restraint. However, I have been advised that the Japanese government intends to keep a close watch on the level of exports of these goods to Canada. We are keeping this particular matter under constant review.

subtopic: CANADIAN VOTE ON RESOLUTION RESPECTING RED CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister how the Canadian delegation, on instructions from his government, voted on the Italian resolution to send the question of the admission of China to the United Nations to a study committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN VOTE ON RESOLUTION RESPECTING RED CHINA
speechtext: As I understand the question it is as to how we voted. We abstained on that question. We felt that the establishment of a committee was a tactic which would result in delay in action on the matter. Because we want to be in a position on this question, as on others, and to be able to act freely if as a result of our review that is what we decide to do, we preferred to abstain rather than submit the whole question to a committee as suggested by the Italian resolution. That resolution would, perhaps, have the effect of delaying our own possible actions.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: QUEBEC-PROPOSED CHANGE IN NAME OF LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, everyone learned yesterday that the Quebec government is about to change the name of the legislature to that of National Assembly of the province of Quebec. According to the Prime Minister, is there any constitutional objection to this new name and could he tell us his reaction to this report?

subtopic: QUEBEC-PROPOSED CHANGE IN NAME OF LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
As to my reaction, Mr. Speaker-and that may spare me the trouble of answering the first part of the question, which is a legal question-I think that the province of Quebec considers doing what it has a right to do under the constitution, that is amend its own provincial constitution, with the exception of the office of lieutenant governor.
As far as the name is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is cause for alarm. The province of Ontario has also changed the name of its legislature by calling it the parliament of Ontario. The name of the members of the Ontario provincial legislature have also been changed, I believe, and they are now members of the provincial parliament. speakeroldname: Hon. Bryce S. Mackasey (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first occasion I have had to present the estimates of any department to this house. I welcome the opportunity not only of explaining what my department is doing but also of course, of listening to the observations and views of hon. members from other parties in the house as well as from my own party.
I point out at the beginning of my remarks that the estimates of the Unemployment Insurance Commission were referred to the standing committee and have been dealt with by that appropriate committee and accepted.
Earlier in the session, during the throne speech debate, I had an opportunity to express my philosophy and views on the collective bargaining system that prevails in Canada. I detailed the record of successes of that system in the areas under federal jurisdiction and pointed out that of the 100-odd cases that had been referred to the Department of Labour where strikes could possibly have ensued, there were strikes in only six cases, only two of those being of major consequence.
I would be misleading the house if I suggested that changes are not needed in the legislation concerning industrial relations. It is no longer sufficient to react to situations. Rather, we must anticipate them. We must
November 21, 1968

initiate and encourage a much greater degree of communication between labour and management. My department must make sure that labour and management appreciate that they are not natural enemies but, rather, natural partners. In the final analysis the private enterprise system which provides dividends for company shareholders also provides the jobs for our ever-growing labour force as well as the standard of living to which many of us have become accustomed.
There is much activity these days in the department, Mr. Chairman. In anticipation of the Woods Task Force report officials of the department are reviewing existing legislation, preparing new laws and evaluating new concepts in order that we may take advantage of this report and the enlightened approach I hope it will have to the labour problem of today.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that my department must lead; it must encourage labour and management to co-operate more fully. It is my belief that the time has come for the establishment of a new mediation service, a mediation branch composed of experts, experts supported by a proper team of researchers with a detailed knowledge of the industries coming within the federal sphere. I believe that this type of expertise will be of invaluable service to management and labour. These experts could introduce a degree of continued communication between management and labour that should reduce the areas of friction and supply the assistance needed to make collective bargaining more meaningful.
Until the Woods task force report is tabled, Mr. Chairman, hon. members can understand my reluctance to discuss at this time the many changes in detail that I believe are necessary if my department is to assume its full role in the just society of tomorrow.
I have had an opportunity while reviewing my department to acquaint myself with many of the problems facing Canada and Canadians today, problems that in some direct or indirect way concern or should concern the Department of Labour. I am concerned, for instance, about work stoppages and disputes that are prolonged far beyond the point where anyone stands to gain. I am concerned about the lack of communication within the trade union movement itself, as evidenced by the increasing number of cases where the general union membership has failed to ratify agreements entered into by its own leadership.
Supply-Labour
I am concerned that quite often this failure to ratify agreements is the direct result of the negotiating team presenting exorbitant and extravagant demands. The same union leaders then wonder why the rank and file reject the negotiated settlement after they have irresponsibly built up the anticipation of their membership.
I am not suggesting that exaggerated demands are the only reason for the rejection of negotiated settlements, but they certainly are a contributing factor. I think that in the main responsible union leaders will agree with me that they must communicate more effectively, more reasonably with their membership and impress upon them the fact that wage increases cannot consistently outstrip productivity without eventually bringing about a reduction in the standard of living. I am not at all surprised when the public expresses indignation on learning through the news media that a union is demanding a 15 or 20 per cent wage increase per year.
I am also concerned about the welfare of that third segment of Canadian society-not management, not the unions, but the unorganized worker and the senior citizen, people on fixed incomes, the blind, the crippled, the disabled, people who are not represented at the bargaining table. I often wonder when management divide up the profit between dividends and increased salaries whether they should not stop to think if some of these exorbitant or large profits should not reflect lower prices, whether there should not be a greater social awareness of the responsibility of organized labour as well as of management to the unorganized segment to which I have already alluded.
Ability to pay must not be the only criterion for settlement at the bargaining table. There is a growing social responsibility resting on both Canadian management and unions, and I suggest to them that they begin to demonstrate a greater consciousness of this responsibility.
I would like to speak very briefly on the work of conciliation boards. Over the years conciliation boards have served the public of Canada well in settling, or making recommendations which assist in the settlement of, labour disputes. They continue to serve and have done very effective work as recently as the current fiscal year. However, I am disturbed at a growing practice that seems to prevail, namely that when a conciliation board has failed to settle a dispute it then

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
submits a report containing no recommendations, in effect returning the issue to the protagonists with no guide lines or suggestions whatsoever, and which quite often reflects a minimum of effort by the board to resolve the dispute.
I am not unaware that this action is often requested by the parties, but regardless of arguments which may be advanced in favour of this tactic, it seems to me it reflects an abdication of responsibility on the part of the chairmen of such boards and the representatives of management and labour.
On the whole, Mr. Chairman, I am proud of the contribution made by conciliation boards, but I can foresee the day when the appointment of a board in labour disputes may become the exception rather than the rule. This will mean an expanded role for our conciliation officers and should impress upon the parties the necessity of reaching an accommodation at the conciliation officer stage.
Members might forgive me if I devote some time at this stage of my remarks to the question of automation, of technological change, and of the growing and pressing need for increased productivity in Canada.
There was a time, of course, when increased productivity was a simple matter: one supplied his help with a larger shovel or a bigger wheelbarrow. But today increased productivity is synonymous with technological change, with automation, with sophisticated methods of production. Because of our great reliance on exports to maintain our standard of living and to absorb our ever-growing labour force, we must accept and indeed seek out these advanced methods of production if we are to compete with such countries as West Germany, Japan, Sweden and the United States.
We talk about a just society. A just society, to this Liberal at any rate, means a society where medicare is a right and not a privilege, a society where decent housing is not a luxury but a necessity, a society with a decent standard of living for those less fortunate among us. I refuse to accept the concept that a country like Canada, with its tremendous assets, raw materials, highly skilled labour force and free enterprise system, cannot afford these things. To be unable to provide these things to our citizens can only be described as a failure of the system we endorse in this country. I suggest the free enterprise system is on trial in Canada and must measure up to the challenge of supplying these
[Mr. Mackasey.l
rights. The solution is not in the elimination of medicare or other social measures that have made Canada synonymous with an enlightened attitude toward its people, but in rallying our energies, our imagination and our confidence so that the programs can be paid for and carried forward by the fruits of increased productivity.
We must constantly remind ourselves that in many of the nations that we compete with the degree of co-operation that is now needed in Canada, but is lacking at the moment between labour and management, and the amount of planning that is needed not only between labour and management but with government as well, are already a way of life. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, in Japan it is almost a religious cult.
Canadian workers when trained and provided with equal opportunities, equal equipment, equally efficient management and equal markets can meet the production of any industrial worker in the world. But if increased productivity depends on our willingness to accept technological change-and I believe it does-then we must be prepared to face squarely the disruptive forces that technological change creates. Management, of course, accepts quite readily technological change, and why not? In most cases it means survival in an ever-increasingly competitive world. In many other instances it means a greater margin of profit.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
But the acceptance of technological change is still resisted and indeed feared by certain segments of our labour force. Upon reflection, Mr. Chairman, why not? Balanced against the realization that these changes are necessary is the realization by labour that all too often the disruptive forces of technological change are borne solely by the labour class. Why is it always the individual Canadian worker who must bear exclusively the terribly personal and disruptive effects that quite naturally stem from technological change? Surely this cannot be accepted as inevitable, as just, in this year of 1968. Canadian society and its government cannot be so passive, so unconcerned as to accept as part of the game this human disruption.
The Canada-United States auto pact is a perfect example of how management fails to understand its moral obligations to its workers. When close to 500 workers were notified last week-I think that fortunately the figures are now 388-that they were to be laid off by the Ford Motor Company in Windsor, they
November 21, 1383

were given precisely one week's notice, one week to adjust mentally to the impact of layoff, one week to seek out help and advice from the Unemployment Insurance Commission and from the manpower centres, to find out if they qualified for additional benefits or, in too many cases, if they qualified for any type of benefit. I believe that management cannot expect the respect of labour and the full co-operation that is needed unless it begins to assume the moral obligation that technological change and increased productivity involve. I think the time has come for the Minister of Labour to convince his colleagues that legislation defining and emphasizing management's responsibility to its employees in the area of technological change is long overdue.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, the philosophy of Judge Freedman and others like Judge Laskin is clear and precise. There are ways and means of introducing negotiation on technical change without usurping management's right to manage. I am committed to such legislation and am waiting to see what the Woods task force may offer as a method of solution in this very senstitive but highly important area.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I may be allowed to turn to another area that comes under the Department of Labour and which is of growing concern to all Canadians. That is the problem of prejudice and discrimination in the working force of Canada. To me this is an intolerable situation, and we cannot excuse it on any grounds whatsoever. As long as it exists it means that we have Canadians who, in effect, have a special set of working conditions imposed upon them regardless of the laws we pass to equalize rewards and opportunities. A review of existing legislation in my department indicates to me that some substantial amendments are required, and this will be done after careful analysis of the recommendations of the royal commission on the status of women.
Hear, hear.

There are people in this country who have been discriminated against for so long that they have begun to discriminate against themselves, to limit their own aspirations because they cannot conceive that the better opportunities, the better way of life, could be for them also. This is a loss to Canada, a loss to our labour force which we can ill afford.
Supply-Labour
With the intent of fighting prejudice through positive action we have recently set up a branch in the department that intends to enforce as vigorously as possible the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act and to amend it so as to make it more effective. In the meantime officers of this branch have been touring Canada educating employers to the fact that the Department of Labour will not tolerate prejudice based on colour, religion or national origin. To make this campaign effective will require the full support of the unions of this country, as well as the full support of my cabinet colleagues and, I am sure, of all my colleagues in the house.
Above all, Mr. Chairman, I think it is time that the federal government and the crown corporations be model employers, examples for others throughout the country.
Hear, hear.

Now, Mr. Chairman, not being aware as precisely as I should of my role in this discussion of estimates I would conclude by reminding the committee once again that I will not be deterred from my determination to make the Department of Labour a reflection of the new spirit of co-operation and communication that is so badly needed in this country. I will not hesitate to arm it with the legislation it requires to make it an effective instrument, not of labour, not of management, but of the people of Canada, people who are entitled to maximum effort on the part of labour, of government and of management to seek the solutions to increased productivity, to industrial peace and to a just society.
Although most of my remarks today have concerned the department's role in industrial relations and fair employment practices, it will be obvious to hon. members, when we consider the details of the votes, that the department has many and diverse responsibilities and programs. These include the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, the Canada Labour (Safety) Code, the program of the women's bureau, the labour-management consultation program, the annuities branch, and an expanding program of economics and research, just to mention only a few. All of these elements will be caught up in the revitalization and re-positioning of the department to play its optimum role in today's society. To do what I believe must be done will require changes in the structure of the Department of Labour, both in Ottawa and in the various regions, to improve internal communications and flexibility of operations so that it

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
can respond better to public needs and priorities.
Above all, I want to bring the Department of Labour and its services as close as possible to the community it serves. I want to make it more sensitive to the needs of that community. And I want it to become more actively involved as a true partner of management, labour and the public interest.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that there is no room in the statute books of Canada for compulsory arbitration. I think we can achieve the type of industrial peace needed to make this country prosperous by co-operation among the government, labour and management. This is the dedication which I have and with which I shall approach my role as Minister of Labour.

Mr. Chairman, I did not have the slightest intention of taking part in this discussion except that it seemed to me- and I hope the minister will accept this as not being offensive-that he has lectured everybody else and so he might not mind a slight lecture from me directed toward himself and his colleagues. If I understood him correctly he was rather critical of unions, at least of some trade unions, for asking too much in the way of wage increases. I think this is in part due to the inflation psychology in this country and the fear of the working men of what they will be faced with in connection with rising costs of living. I suggest it would be more helpful if members of the government, including this minister, would spend less time lecturing the public in this connection and do a little more themselves to bring inflation under control.
For example, since I have been in this house we have had optimistic statements of activity from ministers of the government, beginning last fall. Last winter, in the depth of the crisis in which the government found itself, the then prime minister gave some assurance on new measures that were being taken, but no action has followed. Since then we have been promised a white paper with regard to an anti-inflationary program and we are still waiting for it. In all seriousness I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that a lecture from the Minister of Labour is a pretty poor substitute for a constructive program from the government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Does the Leader of the Opposition not think it was a good idea for the minister to lecture his own colleagues as to the improvements

that ought to be made on that side of the house?

I do not think he spent enough time lecturing his own colleagues. I think he spent too much time lecturing the public and I am suggesting to him, and through him to his colleagues, that a little more by way of example on their part might be more productive than some of this lecturing that is going on.
Mr. Chairman, I remind the Leader of the Opposition that since we are dealing with estimates I might spend a little time lecturing him before we are through.
Hear, hear.

A very arrogant Minister of Labour.
9 (3:50 p.m.)

Well, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friends down here have so very little to applaud that I do not object to their reacting to that kind of bravado on behalf of the Minister of Labour. I am always delighted to receive any good wishes or anything else he may care to pass my way. However, I believe in all sincerity it is high time the government carried out some of its assurances concerning anti-inflationary programs rather than lecturing members of the public for reacting in the light of their own fears respecting continued inflation.
The minister spoke about the need to anticipate developments and the need for improved methods of achieving industrial peace. We will look forward to hearing about these, presumably following the Woods report and further reflection on the part of the minister. I for one will await them with very keen interest because again I say that we hear these things but see very little action.
The minister spoke of the importance of increased productivity. He stated that in a country like ours we ought to be able to finance enlightened social measures and that we must place the necessary emphasis on productivity in order to achieve these necessary measures. I agree with this unquestionably but I suggest to him, sir, through you, that when one talks about productivity one must not only lecture management and labour but must remember that it is also a question to a considerable degree of having an enlightened government policy. A continued increase in productivity, for example, requires an adequate standard of government services in the field of education throughout our various provinces. I suggest to him that the very hard
November 21, 1968



line he and his colleagues have adopted with regard to the provinces and the effect that this line, if maintained, will have on the services related to productivity which the provincial governments must provide in this country, will have a very unfortunate effect in respect of increasing productivity in Canada.
I suggest it is not merely free enterprise which is on trial in this regard; it is also the government of this country which is on trial. In order to achieve the necessary standard of government services throughout the country a degree of co-operation is required rather than a hard line which amounts almost to dictation from the federal government. It is necessary for the two levels of government to achieve some understanding in connection with priorities rather than have one level of government simply resort to lectures.
The minister spoke about discrimination. I certainly share his concern and disapproval of any discrimination which exists. Unfortunately it does exist in this country. He referred particularly to discrimination based on race, religion, creed or something of that sort. People in one part of the country may feel there is discrimination because they happen to live in a certain part of the country. I am sure the minister also has this in mind. I should like to suggest that discrimination cannot be eliminated simply by the passage of legislation to ban discrimination. If in this country we are to achieve the elimination of discrimination, which as I see it really amounts to achieving something like equality of opportunity, much more than anti-discriminatory legislation is required. I suggest we must have a very well oriented program working toward something like achievement of equality of opportunity involving education, the overcoming of traditional handicaps and the overcoming of discrimination, if you like, which results from poor housing. All these things have been mentioned by a good many Canadians.
I point out that discrimination of this kind certainly will not be overcome simply by any legislation the minister may have in mind. Again it is essential, if we are too make any real progress in respect of overcoming discrimination in this country, that the government be prepared to work out an effective system of co-operation with the provinces so that the government can work together with the provinces to overcome discrimination.
Before I sit down I should like to say that if the government continues to pursue the hard line it is taking, what we will see will not be the elimination of discrimination but
Supply-Labour
rather a vast increase in discrimination in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the minister to his new portfolio and wish him well in his work. He gives every indication of being a man who is dedicated to the well-being particularly of the labouring people in this country and also, as he says, all Canadians. I only hope that the legislation he supports, both in the house and more particularly in cabinet, will lead to the realization of the principles in which he says-and I believe he does-he believes.
Earlier this afternoon he gave some indication that, from the point of view of those of us in this party at least, he is clearly moving in the right direction. I refer of course to his attitude in respect of the Freedman report. Having said that, I should like to take this opportunity to raise briefly two matters of policy orientation to which I should like the minister to give very careful consideration.
First I should like to say a few words about unemployment. I hope the Minister of Labour will concern himself with what is almost certain to be in store for us during the coming winter. If past and present trends continue we will experience one of the worst winters in recent years. It was not many years ago that economists considered a 3 per cent unemployment level as the absolute maximum for any advanced industrial society that wished to maintain any kind of civilized existence. At no time in the past three years, however, have we had a national unemployment level as low as 3 per cent. In the Atlantic provinces the lowest quarterly level was 5.8 per cent. That was in the spring of 1966. Again, considering the national average, if we begin with the first quarter of 1966 and look at the succeeding quarterly levels of unemployment we see a continuous increase, with not one quarterly decline, from 3.3 per cent in the winter of 1966 to 5.1 per cent for the third quarter of this year.
These figures are bad enough, but they are even more alarming when they are broken down into regions. For example, unemployment in the Atlantic provinces during this same period increased from 6.7 per cent to 8 per cent and in Quebec from 4.7 per cent to 6.5 per cent. Again we get a more precise picture of the deplorable level of unemployment for an advanced industrial society by looking at the peak winter months. In the Atlantic provinces in January, 1967, 9.9 per cent of the labour force was without work. In January, 1968, the figure was 10.9. Now, given

November 21, 1963
Supply-Labour
the increase of unemployment this year over last, it would not be unreasonable to forecast that unemployment in the Atlantic provinces will reach a level of 12 per cent or 13 per cent this coming January.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I could go on producing these alarming figures from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics but I think my point has been made. We in Canada are experiencing an alarming level of unemployment and the government, far from introducing programs aimed at alleviating the situation, is actually aggravating it. First, we received the announcement that the winter works program was to be abolished. Then we had the Minister of Finances' conservative chamber of commerce budget, the main effect of which will be to reduce even farther the level of employment. Not content with cutting back on government spending, the Minister of Finance imposed a new regressive tax. By reducing both government and private purchasing power the minister did just about all he could to maximize unemployment levels during the coming winter. I mention unemployment during the discussion of the labour department's estimates because it should be a major responsibility of the Minister of Labour and, of course, the minister of manpower to get their cabinet colleagues to do something about the alarming situation.
While I am on this matter, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if he would produce for the house his department's unemployment forecast for the coming winter. I should like him to present figures for each of the provinces and for each of our major cities.
I should like to take this opportunity to say something about what is probably the central issue of an industrial society, namely, the relationship between capital and labour, between the few who own our industries and the many who work for them.
I think I may be saying something with which the minister will find himself in substantial agreement. It is clear that in Canada today it is as true as it ever was that when the worker faces his boss, whether in the form of owner or manager, he does not do so as an equal. The emergence and development of trade unions in Canada in the past decades have substantially improved the position of the worker. Provided he is a member of a union, he no longer can be fired at the whim of his employer; nor are his wages and supplementary benefits at the low level they would otherwise be. Notwithstanding these

tangible and important benefits, Canada's unionized workers, not to mention the majority who are not union members, are not and cannot be in a position of equality with their employers. If they were, each would have the same say in production decisions, in policies involving the allocation of capital, and in discussions concerning the nature and price of the product.
No serious student of industrial relations would claim that labour and management are on equal ground in these areas. Indeed, most people accept almost as a self-evident truth that they should not be equal in respect to these matters. Decisions about production, the allocation of capital, and the nature and price of the product, according to the prevailing ideology quite properly belong to the owners or their appointees, the managers. The men who own the shares, it is argued, not only have the final say about what goes on in the factory but, as well, it is proper that they do so. Unfortunately most people in Canada think this way.
So long as this situation and attitude prevail, Mr. Chairman, it is a mockery of reality to assert as many do that management and labour are partners in industry. Those who use the phrase imply that there is a state of equality between the two. Such a phrase is part of that political vocabulary whose purpose is not to elucidate reality but to obscure it. It is used by those who seek to persuade us that the basic structure of the existing economic order in Canada is a just one. We must not be taken in, Mr. Chairman. The central structure and its entailed power relations of our economic system are unequal; they are unjust.
In one sense the history of the trade union movement in Canada can be seen as an attempt by our workers to break down the barriers to equality. They have sought to make inroads on the so-called rights of management. They have sought to have more control over their own day to day fives. The most recent example of this struggle for equality is the attempt to have some say in the introduction of new technology and work practices in industry.
At present in Canada our workers are entirely dependent upon the whim of their employers. During the course of a signed contract management can introduce a new machine or an alternative practice whose effects might be devastating for the workers. Workers can do nothing about them from a legal point of view.
November 21, 1988

Why is this? The reason, Mr. Chairman, is that the main thrust of Canadian labour law makes it so. Most arbitrators in labour disputes have based their rulings on the residual rights theory of industrial relations. What this theory means is that an employer retains the rightful power to do whatever he wishes with his business enterprise except with regard to those rights he has specifically yielded to a union in a written contract. It also means that the trade unionist can do only what is precisely stipulated in the contract. Unless a union can indicate that the relevant contract forbids some activity, whether it be a re-arrangement of time schedules or the introduction of automated equipment, management can do what it wills. Unless the contract specifically permits the worker to do something, he can do nothing.
Obviously even the most ably led union is not clairvoyant. It is impossible to tell in advance what new production technique management might introduce during the duration of the contract. Not having this knowledge, no union can make the required specific contract demands in advance.
Furthermore, unlike the situation in other industrial nations, for example, in the United States and the United Kingdom, in Canada unions do not have the right to strike during the period covered by the contract. If during this period they object to some new practice, they must resort to arbitration. Most arbitrators, as I indicated-there are exceptions- rely on the residual rights theory. Consequently, as one labour expert, Mr. Ed Finn, observed recently, "99 times out of a hundred" the union loses in disputes in this area.
For many years now the unilateral power bestowed on the owners of industry by the residual rights principle has meant thousands of Canadian workers have been badly treated. They have lost seniority rights, their jobs, and on occasion even their community. Their lives, in short, have been profoundly and adversely affected by this principle. It is a remarkable fact that Canadian workers are feeling its impact and are beginning to demand a share in the decision-making process. All Canadians, whether in unions or not, should note and be proud of this fact. What workers are beginning to say is, we should as human beings have more control over our destiny and over day to day issues that affect our lives. Can anyone deny the moral legitimacy of that claim?
Three years ago Mr. Justice Freedman presented a report on labour relations to the
Supply-Labour
government of the day. As many of us know, his report arose out of an investigation into a wildcat strike by thousands of Canadian National Railways employees. The workers had been objecting to unilateral action by the management of Canadian National Railways. As we all know, and as successive Liberal ministers of labour have known for three years, Mr. Justice Freedman made some crucial and, I think, beneficial recommendations. Among these were, first, that the residual rights theory in arbitration matters be discarded; second, that management be obliged to negotiate all major work changes with the unions; and third, that unions be given the right to strike during the period of time covered by a contract.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
It is a sad fact that the government which brought the Freedman report into being chose to ignore it, as have subsequent governments. It is even sadder that three successive ministers of labour have, at least hitherto, done nothing about it. The present Minister of Labour, in a speech delivered on October 8 in Toronto, expressed agreement with Mr. Justice Freedman, as he did earlier today. In that speech of last month he said it is "clear that big business today has a moral responsibility, before introducing technological changes, to make sure these changes cause the minimum of disruption, that they are revealed soon enough to make certain that employees have the time and opportunity to adjust to these changes." The Minister of Labour went on to say that he hoped "this moral obligation becomes more and more apparent to management."
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, where was the moral obligation of the Ford Motor Company which informed hundreds of workers just a few days ago that within a week they would no longer have a job? Is this any way to treat a working man? It does not matter at what level of society he is or what occupation he follows; this is no way to treat a human being. This is immoral behaviour, not moral responsibility. Are we in Canada to wait for the moral regeneration of the directors of the Ford Motor Company? We might just as well wait for the second coming, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Labour and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration are apparently genuinely quite angry with the Ford Motor Company with regard to this matter. I hope their anger is sufficient to lead to government action.

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
If we had always taken the advice of our past and present ministers of labour we would never have passed a good deal of the social and labour legislation in this country. If moral exhortation worked we would never have needed trade unions in the first place; we would not now require minimum wage laws. The list could be extended almost without limit with regard to labour and social welfare measures. We simply cannot rely upon the good will of people to do what ought to be done.
The present Minister of Labour has been wrong to rely in the past upon the voluntary co-operation of industry. The fact that a few employers have agreed to negotiate work change clauses in their contracts with unions in no way counters the need for mandatory law in this area. It will take far too long for all our unionized workers to receive the right that justice requires if we wait for the will of all employers to be tested. If we do this, we will be waiting for a very long time.
I am near the conclusion of my remarks, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps the most significant recommendation of the Freedman report is that workers be given the right to strike during the period of a contract. This right is long overdue. As I said, it now exists in most other industrial countries. It is important if the other right recommended in the Freedman report, the right to negotiate work changes during the contract, is to have any meaning. Unless workers have the right to strike during the course of the contract they will make almost no headway in negotiating work changes during the contract period. Therefore this is, if you like, the key recommendation; workers must have the right to strike during the period of a contract.
The decisive issue for Canadian labouring men and women in the years ahead is whether or not they are to cease being among the manipulated instruments in the productive process. They must not become the victims of technological change. Rather, we need laws that will allow them to continue their struggle for control of their own fate. The immediate implementation of the Freedman report would be a step in this direction.

Mr. Chairman, a great many matters come to mind in the course of this debate on the estimates of the Department of Labour, such as the working conditions of those lucky enough to hold a job during the present unemployment crisis, a proper balance between equitable salaries and the rising cost
[Mr. Broadbent.l
of living, the search for methods to allow the greatest possible number of workers to find suitable jobs, the necessity of keeping up with the evolution of modem techniques in the production of necessary goods with the least physical effort, and the role of the trade union movement in present-day society. Much could be said on many subjects which are all related to labour.
Unless one completely lacks a sense of observation, one must recognize that everything that has been done in the world has been done by labour, organized or not. The unfortunate thing today is that this whole army of workers is too often faced with problems of crisis, strikes, unemployment, automation or taxes, to mention only a few.
We seem to have forgotten that work is not the be-all and end-all of life, but rather a means of ensuring for the worker a decent standard of living and a normal stability thanks to the equitable division of responsibilities among everybody.
The direction of an important department such as the Department of Labour involves great responsibilities and requires the cooperation of impartial and competent advisers. I sincerely wish the present minister the health and clear-sightedness necessary to find the most appropriate solutions at the proper time.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We are too easily content with a good word here and there when work is being discussed, which leaves the impression that we accept it as a necessary evil of the human condition. Yet, work often contributes to shaping, and often, to saving man. Work gives him, with dignity, the freedom which ennobles him.
The working man usually pursues various goals. First of all, he wants to earn a living for himself and his family. He wishes to be independent, self-sufficient. He feels less of a man when he depends on others in a way that is not legitimate. Because man is reasonable, he derives a certain satisfaction from doing something for himself. The worker is proud to be someone, to accomplish something and to help others. He wants to have a place in the world. He is proud of being useful. Through his moral interest and brotherly help, he contributes to the expansion of civilization.
It is normal for a worker to aspire to belonging to a labour group that cares about his needs and favours the progress of society as a whole, working efficiently towards its various goals.
November 21, 1968

At the present time, the worker is struggling with a difficult situation. There are three possible solutions. The first is the capitalistic solution: benefits for the few, toil and sweat for the others. The second is the collectivist solution: benefits for the State, toil and sweat for all men. The third is the Christian solution: benefits for all, toiling by all. Sharing, that is what we need.
Business, formerly moral, has now been replaced by business morals. Indeed, a solution to labour problems and economic life as a whole is sought in the advice given to everyone: make as much money as possible, maximize profit at the lowest possible cost, to allow limitless competition.
This is what happens: The merchant sells at the highest possible price, while purchasing at the lowest, and he often earns three or four times more than the one who labours to produce.
Management tries to purchase raw materials at the lowest possible cost, and to pay the lowest possible salaries while trying to sell goods for the best possible price.
The worker often tries to work as little as possible and at times-which is unfortunate- as little as possible while trying to get the highest salary possible. This cannot go on. The class struggle is an egotistic struggle, and an autocratic, over-powerful state could not solve our problems. What is needed is an economic order inspired by social justice, having the same regard for business prosperity and fair wages, while taking the legitimate interests of the consumer and the seller into consideration.
In our modern world, virtually no one can produce alone all the goods needed for one's keep. Labour is partitioned to a degree, and increasingly specialized, which contributes to an abundant over-all production.
Would we be stupid enough, with all the modern means available to us, to proclaim ourselves unable to distribute our own production? Experience has shown that we have very good reasons to advocate the means which we know: the Social Credit. Though obviously not a panacea, it certainly is a step in the right way. If our politicians know of other means, let them apply them without delay because a great percentage of our people are tired of this succession of strikes, of battles between unions, of an inoperative labour legislation.
It is easy to see that our legislative system lacks flexibility in the field of labour management relations. Those long delays with regard
Supply-Labour
to negotiations and the renewal of collective agreements show without any doubt that the system is unhealthy and when many conflicts arise too many physicians who seem unable to agree on a cure gather around the sick bed.
I recall that Dr. Marius Barnard, the brother of the famous South African surgeon Christian Barnard, who had successfully completed a heart transplant operation, put it very aptly and briefly in those words: A new heart to change a heartless world.
We often find that we only react fleetingly to the many cases of misery resulting from job insecurity, insufficient income, the fear of tomorrow which is often the root of many disorders. We seem unable to abolish misery through a more equitable distribution of responsibility.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I will deal, if I have time to do so, with the problem of unemployment, the terms of the regulations of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the centralization of offices and other matters concerning the workers.
I would like to mention now the disastrous results of the ever increasing number of strikes which have become more popular than the miniskirt. Today some workers-even students, the workers of tomorrow-seem under the impression that to be hip they must stage their own little strike. They should stop however and think about the end result, even if they are hip. The helm must be kept steady, should a storm come up.
A few strikes here and there are nothing unusual. But when the industry or the services are paralysed so long and so often, something has gone seriously wrong.
This leads me to quote from an article which is worth thinking over. It was written by Father Yvan Morin and published in a newspaper of our area, Le Saint-Laurent, in February 1967, under the title "Have we all gone mad or are we totally immature?" It reads partly as follows:
Even today, strikes seem a necessary and legal means, but the fact that we have to resort frequently to that ultimate means is indicative of the climate of immaturity in which we live.
It is necessary and legal for policemen to carry a gun, but the day when they will use it casually will be a dark day indeed; either we will have become a nation of gangsters, or policemen will be irresponsible.
The proliferation of strikes reveals either a craving for economic dictatorship within the industrial world or unreasonable demands on the part of union members. We must realize that we all have rights and obligations, that we are all each other servants.
3C24

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
One of the major malaises today, stems from the fact that little store is set by government authority.
Is it then not worthy of respect? Do we no longer understand the meaning of authority? Anyhow, the government cannot boast of the part it has played in labour disputes-
Looking more closely at the situation, we find that there are various kinds of strikes which we may divide into four categories.
First, there are strikes that could be called "backlog" strikes, because of strained relations between employers and workers, and also because of the practice of always of waiting until the strike is called before taking a decision.
The second type of strikes are the prestige strikes; as a matter of fact, some people derive great satisfaction in proclaiming they have won a battle even at the expense of the workers.
The third class comprises political strikes; unfortunately some sectarians seem to gloat over long drawn-out strikes, quite obviously to embarrass political parties which have not always taken their suggestions to seriously.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In the fourth place, the necessary strikes, those that are spontaneously approved by the majority of workers, after all honest means of persuasion have been used up. If we had to put up with strikes of that type only, things would look much brighter.
The important thing is to locate the numerous causes of misunderstanding and to steer labour legislation towards the protection of the rights of the weak, of the small people, of the poor, of all those who need that protection most. Let us note, by the way, that complicated laws often breed confusion.
It is to the advantage of workers that present and future labour leaders should know about their rights and duties so as to preserve those rights and fulfill their duties.
The education of workers must be directed by union leaders conscious of their responsibilities, in a realistic spirit of understanding, working like partners for the development of the country. Their efforts must not be limited to those of simple pressure groups interested in their own material profits, to the prejudice of national, provincial or municipal interests.
It is normal for union leaders to fight in order that their members might receive a fair economic retribution; they must also keep in mind the interests and the needs of the whole country and use their authority with a vision of the future and for a social purpose.

Any responsible observer will admit that unions have sprung from a need which is still making itself felt. Having been a union member for several years, as well as the president of local 2817 of the Quebec Brotherhood of carpenters, woodworkers, lumbermen and sawmill employees for 10 years-from 1952 to 1962-I make no bones about saying that to my mind a strike is not the natural and easy way to smooth out difficulties in relations between management and labour. Only through a complete lack of imagination could one think that a series of mistakes can be cancelled by a new set of planned errors. The parties concerned should listen to reason and act like adults. In a democratic country, every citizen can state his views and can even hope that they will be respected; however, he should show sufficient understanding for the ideas of others.
People are struggling to obtain salary increases to catch up with the missing dollars without worrying too much where they come from, who controls them and how their value is determined. What is the use of earning $3 or more an hour if a dollar is only worth 35 cents?
This is a problem of the distribution of wealth, purchasing power, work and leisure time. Some order must be brought about in this inefficient financial system.
Let us imagine here a problem of distribution among children. There are two apples to be shared among ten children: the strongest one will win the fight and get the apples. In the case of two apples to be divided among ten children having some money, the highest bidder will win, provided he is under police protection. However, when there are fifteen apples and ten children, every child will have one and everybody will be satisfied.
This sums up the present crisis. We are acting like children.
The purchasing power must be re-established on the basis of demand and the value of wealth, while taking into account that energy consuming work is gradually replaced by machines. The worker craves for money in order to earn his living and that of his dependants. He should be treated fairly so that he does not have to walk around carrying slogan-bearing signs.
The present application of our labour legislation is lacking in flexibility and appears powerless to intervene in the increasing number of disastrous strikes affecting the country's economy. Therefore, we, of the Rallie-ment Creditiste, recommend that additional
November 21, 1968

powers be included in the labour legislation to implement the establishment of an impartial and "genuine labour tribunal" made up of representatives of labour, management and government.
This tribunal, made up of experts in the field of labour management relations, would have to have the proper powers and information to be able to:
(1)	Avoid interunion conflicts, by establishing a specific and clear procedure in order to determine, through secret ballot, under the supervision of two members from the tribunal, the right to representation of the workers by a union in good faith;
(2)	Determine a period of negotiations not exceeding 90 days, and establish severe penalties for those who do not observe the rules;
(3)	Make a proper assessment of the business or service returns, taking into account risks, monetary reserves required for the upkeep of the business, tax deductions and procedures resulting from taxation rules;
(4)	Determine, when needed, a job classification that would take into account the responsibilities of each class of workers, a salary range commensurate with the business or service potentialities and measured according to the cost of living index;
(5)	Require that all strike votes be taken by secret ballot, under the supervision of two members of the labour tribunal, and that the strike be deemed legal only if it has been accepted by 50 per cent plus 1 of the business' employees, and only after all other means of conciliation have been exhausted.
(6)	Guide negotiations in the field of public services in such a way as to determine salary adjustments on an hourly rate basis for all those whose salary is under $5,000 a year.
I have met so many railway employees, especially temporary gangs, who were greatly annoyed with the government's decision to have them return to work under practically unchanged conditions, while in their case particularly, they are low wage-earners who get an increase on a percentage basis, which does not suit them. And yet, it seems to me that it was so easy to understand the situation. I see the hon. minister is nodding. I trust that, in a similar situation, he will find the appropriate words to say at the right moment to try and improve this situation.
As to the co-operation between workers and employers, the government must inform people on the best methods existing to maintain harmonious relationship. A great deal of
Supply

Labour
practical work is already being done in this field and I strongly support the efforts of the department in this direction.
In many industries, it should also be possible to encourage through appropriate legislation employers who feel inclined to promote participation of employees to the company's benefits, by allowing them to become coowners or associates, which would create a climate of encouragement.
Before concluding my remarks, I would like to point out a very important matter of concern to a great number of workers of my area who work in the United States. Unfortunately, no agreement has been reached as yet with four American states, especially those which are adjacent to our area, New Hampshire and more particularly, Maine. The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) should take into account the representations we have been making for a very long time.
I remember that, a few years ago, a member of the opposition even staked his seat in order to accelerate the settlement of this problem. I therefore think that it would be only fair that the thousands of Canadian workers who are employed in the United States-and who, in a way, by doing so alleviate the problem of unemployment at home-should benefit from an adequate formula. Such a formula must exist, and I think that if we really try, we shall find it. We shall then be able to give those people the opportunity of getting unemployment insurance benefits when they come back to Canada, once the lumbering operations are over.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
There is also, nowadays, the famous problem of centralization of the offices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In our area, in particular, pressures are exerted in that direction so as to avoid as much as possible this kind of centralization. This should bring abbout the results which we are expecting, because we would have the advantage, as we have had in the past, to meet understanding people. In fact, the enforcement of unemployment insurance regulations which change rather often, is a source of problems. I understand the difficulties faced by the civil servants and I know many of them who are very nice and who try to do their jobs as conscientiously as possible. However, the fact remains that in the light of the regulations arising from the existing legislation, methods are changed every year to the point where the workers cannot keep abreast of all those changes. Therefore, having submitted a

Supply-Labour
claim in proper form, they find it very difficult to get their benefits.
I am aware of this problem. In fact, hundreds of workers come to see me every year, especially during the unemployment season, asking me to help them find a solution. I think that it would be very important to look at this field most carefully.
Therefore, I rely on the co-operation of the minister to find the necessary solutions.

Mr. Chairman, the discussions on the estimates of each department give every Canadian the opportunity to get more interested in the economic affairs of Canada, and to allow more particularly the members to express their opinions on some subjects. As a member, I take a great interest in the expansion of the Canadian economy, and as a representative of the Montreal area and the working class, I am more particularly concerned with the growth of the Montreal harbour.
Indeed, Montreal has the greatest harbour in Canada. Therefore, it is possible to appreciate the importance of its commercial activities. The importance of Montreal harbour is related, in the first place, to its geographic position. This port plays a key role in the international trade of Canada and in the distribution of its imports, while it is a stopover for shipment of our products to foreign countries and for the distribution of our imports.
I take an active interest in Montreal harbour as an essential factor in the vitality of our economy, as an incentive for Montreal trade and as an employer of many residents of my riding. For these three reasons, I think it is essential that Montreal harbour, in its efforts to expand its activities, should arouse the interest of all members and be able to rely on their support.
However, conditions in Montreal harbour are not satisfactory. Indeed, it has been noted for some time that the harbour does not operate at full capacities. We can discuss the various factors that have led to such a situation, but I think there is one that is recognized by all, and that is labour relations which impair the efficiency of the harbour. This has, in fact, led to the work stoppage of 1966. The government then took a practical step to deal with these problems and instituted to this end the Picard commission of inquiry. The report of the commission contains many recommendations dealing with labour relations. It put the blame for this situation on the two parties involved.

It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to recall well-known facts, but I would merely point out the significant contribution of the government towards a meaningful solution.
Following the Picard report, the employers agreed to set up a guarantee fund to provide for a minimum of 35 paid hours per week to 2,157 employees.
I would like, Mr. Chairman, to emphasize the necessity of this work guarantee for the Montreal dockers. Under the old system, the employees depended on the goodwill of management, and there was no guarantee to the worker under any rational system for hiring and distribution of work. I know the workers in my riding and my area, and I know how they react. I know how important a factor security is in work motivation. Full productivity cannot be asked of the worker if he does not know what tomorrow will be like.
More recently still, Maxwell Cohen was commissioned to present a report on labour problems. This report contains a number of steps to be taken by employers, with a view to facilitating the adaptation of workers affected by automation.
A few weeks ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) gave the Union a cheque for $63,000 to provide for implementation of the recommendations of this report.
These various factors reflect the government's concern with respect to the labour disputes problem. I would like to point out here the very valuable contribution of our Minister of Labour.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal briefly with a last important point concerning the explanation of the present situation. Just like any business concern, the Montreal harbour must necessarily keep progressing, and I think that to survive any business must develop its potential to the utmost. However, I think that in a just society, progress must be shared among all citizens. And one of the most significant applications of progress is the introduction of new techniques in industry, and Montreal harbour is no exception to the rule.
I wish to point out the importance and the size of the problem created by the introduction of containers. This new transportation system makes possible increased efficiency in spite of reduced manpower.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I am quite aware that a number of dockers who are eager to retain their jobs do not welcome this prospect. We are facing here two somewhat conflicting situations.
November 21. 1968

On the one hand, employers will have to improve their equipment in order to meet competition, and, as I said, I fully agree with this view. I furthermore suggest that if Canada is anxious to stay abreast of international competition, her industries will have, willy nilly, to bring about new operating methods so as to reduce costs and meet successfully the competition from abroad.
On the other hand, I disagree with the idea of doing so at the expense of labour. Where this particular case is concerned, introducing containers will be a commanding factor, in my opinion, towards improved returns to the Montreal harbour. Indeed, important harbours are increasingly using this method for the shipment of commodities, as it costs much less than the traditional system.
But dockers must not suffer from the introduction of this new equipment. It is becoming universally recognized that when changes affect the workers, employers have a moral obligation toward their employees.
Technological progress must not take place without human progress. In the Montreal harbour, mechanization must not impede the dockers' progress, or labour-management relations.
I also think that a true dialogue is one of the essential conditions for the well-being of the workers, especially when such a change is involved. Such a dialogue must be initiated by the employer, since he is responsible for the change. He must be prepared to discuss the outcome of his action with his employees, through their union.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that it is impossible to hold responsible only one of the parties involved. I believe that the introduction of containers in Montreal harbour must come about through a common effort, as a sign of both technological and human progress.
On the other hand, employees must admit that progress is irreversible, and that any action to stop it brings unpleasant results for everyone.
At first glance, it seems absolutely incomprehensible that employees should want to brake progress. But it is enough to discuss with them and to put oneself in their place to understand that the workers often have no other choice. The majority of them have, just like us, family responsibilities. When they lose their job, they know that they lose their source of income which enables to provide for their needs and that they will have to overcome almost insuperable difficulties to return to the labour market.

Under those circumstances, how can an employee be asked to understand the necessity of progress? The only solution open to him is to hang on to his work which guarantees him a regular income. On the other hand, the employers must understand that phenomenon. The fate of human beings cannot be determined with statistical curves.
The only way to change the attitudes of employers and employees is to improve communications between them. Thus, we can achieve a situation where employees will understand the economic significance of change, and the employers will understand that the human factor must be taken into account in reaching economic decisions. Taking into account the present situation at the Montreal harbour, I am sure that communications need to be improved. As for me, I cannot admit that improvement in the Montreal harbour may mean loss of employment for some people living in my constituency or district.
I also intend to do the utmost to see that the interests of my fellow-citizens are brought to the attention of the house, and I believe that those named to represent the Canadian people should make it a point of honour to try and set things right.
Also I know that our minister of labour is fully conscious of the various factors at stake in the Montreal harbour; he has proved it on several occasions. In fact, the hon. minister never hesitated to fulfill his duty as Minister of Labour in all the disputes and conflicts which occurred since he accepted this position. Furthermore, events have shown that he had the right approach and that he is very popular with both the workers and the employers. On behalf of the workers, I wish to thank him for his devotion and for his efforts with regard to the settlement of labour disputes, he was far-sighted and fair-minded throughout.
In closing, I will say that my feelings for the hon. Minister of Labour are understandable because we both come from the labour class. We both started at the bottom and, today, we have the honour and privilege to sit in the Canadian parliament keeping in mind the motto of Quebec, our native province i "Je me souviens."
May Divine Providence give us health, lucidity and courage to carry on the task which we have undertaken so as not to deceive the hope and confidence placed in us. May it allow us also to see and participate to the fulfillment of our destiny.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment as Minister of Labour. Having regard to the report in the Labour Gazette for September and my own connections with labour, although I cannot aspire to the same heights as the minister and the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve I should like to go back to the time when I was attending college and worked in the coal mines in my area as well as with a pick and shovel for what I might call an upper Canada construction company. Since I have been elected to this house and in experiences in my own area I have certainly had many connections with labour, and I come from an area that employs a large amount of labour.
Although the minister is up to most challenges, what bothers me at this time is that the Department of Labour has been fragmented. Much of the guts has been taken out of it and given to other departments, including the department of manpower. Many of the functions that have been given to the Department of Manpower and Immigration I would prefer to see under the control of the present Minister of Labour, but since that is not the case we have to face the facts. This fragmentation has an unfortunate effect so far as labour is concerned. The various functions and duties relating to labour are now distributed between two departments. The powers and functions of the Department of Labour are [DOT]divided and the department is dangerously weakened.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Many of the relevant functions relating to labour, such as the vital function of maintaining mobility and the upgrading of skills in this age of technology, have been moved to the department of manpower. I hope the Department of Labour has not been downgraded by the government, although this seems to be the case. It has been suggested that the minister is the closest thing to a minister without portfolio, but we hope this is not the case. In the days and weeks ahead we will be watching him to see exactly what he intends to do.
Our duty at this time is to consider these [DOT]estimates in the light of general considerations applying to labour. Thus it is not a matter of considering only the dollars and cents expenditures of the department but of relating its expenditures to labour as a whole in order to ascertain what role the department is playing in the labour field. And again

we are forced to the conclusion that its role has become a minor one. From examination of the blue book I note that the department's functions are limited to collective bargaining and conciliation procedures in industries under federal control, and to research and labour standards. These are important functions, but in the area of a national labour department they are far from all-embracing.
When the original estimates were brought down last session, housing was a part of this department. It is now under the Minister of Transport. There was considerable curiosity about this move when it was first announced. Many people wondered what housing had to do with transport. This has now been explained, since the Minister of Transport has not stopped moving since he took over. But the shortage of housing is still very much part of the labour scene. For instance, housing is related to inflation and to unemployment. As I say, it is very much part of the labour scene considering the effect that housing and its cost have upon the standard of living of Canadian workers. That is why, in the general context of economic conditions as they relate to the situation of labour, we must look at the cost of living, the level of unemployment, the phasing out of training programs and the lack of housing. These are factors that strike at the very roots of labour freedom and mobility.
Dealing with unemployment, the submission of the Canadian Labour Congress to the cabinet last February stated:
Representing as we do, working people across this country, we cannot stress too strongly the gravity with which we view the current economic situation. Once again, it looks as though the burden of poor economic management will be borne by Canadian workers in the form of increasing joblessness.
One may not agree entirely with the C.L.C. at all times but one is forced to agree that present events have borne out its prediction of last February because there is increasing joblessness, as pointed out by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, brought about by government mismanagement, and the burden is being borne by Canadian workers.
Unemployment is a vital factor in labour conditions and labour mobility in this nation. Of course, in respect to an area such as mine, the Atlantic area, and other parts of the country, regional disparity must be mentioned. That is why we must consider the whole field in which labour operates, and one must use this opportunity to ascertain to wha1 extent the government's policies have been
November 21, 1968

effectively applied in the context of unemployment, the cost of living, housing and so on.
Where does one seek out labour policy in this government? Is it in the department of manpower? Is it in the Department of Labour or where is it? Policy is non-existent. Some might mention the Canada Labour Code. This is really a compendium of existing legislation which adds not one whit to the well-being of the working man. What will improve the well-being of the working man is a reduction in the persistently high level of unemployment which has remained at a seasonally adjusted rate of over 5 per cent, the provision of housing which labour can afford, a reduction in the pyramiding cost of living, removal of the iniquitous sales tax, and the restoration of a program of upgrading and training skilled workers. These are the things we must have in order to maintain the position of labour in a world of automated change. The government does not seem to be conscious of this.
I would like to go along with the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby in asking the minister to give a forecast, before this debate concludes, of what the unemployment figures will be this winter, using a computer or anything else. I am thinking especially of areas like Quebec and the Atlantic region. While unemployment in October was over 5 per cent at seasonally adjusted rates, unemployment in the Atlantic provinces was once again the highest in Canada, 5.2 per cent at actual rates not seasonally adjusted. This means that in spite of the government's pious promises and prophecies regional disparity, far from being overcome, is becoming more of a problem each day that the government remains in office.
I suggest that the government has completely neglected the challenge of technological change which is the major challenge facing labour in Canada. I heard what the minister said about the Freedman report, and I concur in that. I think it is a move in the right direction and we will watch it closely. This is just one matter which must be dealt with in order to help the labour force. In ordinary terms the situation can be put this way: We must get with it. Under this government we are not doing enough to help the labour force.
I do not intend to deal with the question of housing in any detail except in the context, as I have said, of labour policy. Last February the government received a memorandum
Supply-Labour
from the Canadian Labour Congress but it paid as much attention to it as it has paid to the various reports of the Economic Council of Canada. In that memorandum the C.L.C.
said:
We believe that all Canadians have a right to decent housing and that governments have an obligation to ensure that it is provided.
What has this government done in respect of housing? We shall have to wait for the Minister of Transport to get his feet back on the ground. The government should have been moving on the question of housing from the time it took office. It should have given a just housing policy to the country.
Canadians cannot afford to have houses at present rates. They cannot afford to buy homes taxed to the tune of about 12 per cent. Surely the government knows that this 12 per cent is pyramided through the whole cost of construction and comes out at the end closer to 20 per cent. The desperate need of Canadians for housing cannot become a matter of profit for lending institutions.
Again I suggest that Canadians must be provided with decent housing. The labour force must be provided with adequate housing. Among other things the government must do much more to provide low rental housing on a much larger scale. Surely the provision of decent housing is part of any consistent labour policy. If the government had any interest in Canadians who work for a living it would have moved long before now.
This afternoon my leader dealt with the matter of inflation. He showed how it cuts down the spending power of the dollar and makes labour unions and workers go after more wages because they require more money. I suggest to the minister that this is one of the most serious challenges of our time, a challenge the government has failed miserably to meet.
Inflation makes the poor poorer. As I said before, it emphasizes regional disparities because the less advanced regions feel the weight of inflation in the same way that the more advanced regions do, and sometimes more seriously because there is no corresponding increase in purchasing power and the disparity increases. In the five years that the government has been in power-
