[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

A Liberal government has been in power for the last five years since 1963. Many Canadians know this too well, especially those in the Atlantic provinces. The Minister of Agriculture is one of these just society ministers. He has put off the agricultural conference until next March. I believe he should have moved justly before now for the farmers of ths country. I shall go into this later when we have the agricultural estimates before us. In the five years since this government has been in power, whether the minister is aware of it or not labour has borne the brunt of the most serious inflation in peacetime history. Food prices alone, for example, during the period have risen by 25 per cent and housing costs have risen an equal amount. I could go further into this subject, but I should like to deal with the matter of conciliation.
I know that in his remarks the minister suggested there should be better mediation practices in this country, and so on. I have a suggestion for him which is based on the postal strike and other strikes which have taken place within the last few months. We also had a long drawn-out grain handlers strike in the course of which the Minister of Agriculture ran around blaming the companies and the Minister of Labour did not move until later. In his statement in the house, I believe in the throne speech debate, he stated why he acted as he did. He may have been correct, although I am not admitting it. However, the six weeks lost because of this disastrous performance have not been regained.
In respect of the postal strike the government allowed the Montpetit report to sit gathering dust for a few years. When the postal workers struck again the members of the government let it go on. My suggestion is that the government should set up a fully autonomous professionally trained conciliation and negotiation commission removed completely from the Treasury Board. That body should go to work a long time before a strike is imminent and not in the last days prior thereto. I believe that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, when speaking on a private member's bill introduced by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, suggested that the present rights of the public service of Canada are now on trial. However, if something like this were done I think many potential strikes probably would not occur although under the legislation the employees are justifiably given this right.

I could go into what are essential services but I shall not do so at this time. The minister spoke of the Woods task force. We will be waiting to see what this task force brings forward. I was interested to read an item which appeared in the Canadian Chamber of Commerce Newsletter for the month of November. It states:
H. D. Woods, M.A., LL.D., Dean, Faculty of Arts and Sciences, McGill University, heads the minister's task force on labour relations. At the annual meeting he confined his remarks largely to the issues before the task force because "we are not yet in a position to present publicly any recommendations since our primary responsibility is to the government."
He pointed out that what is at stake is not whether strikes are to be permitted or not, but whether the whole system of the private decisionmaking for individuals, unions and employers is to be preserved and strengthened by policy and administrative reforms or to be emasculated by creeping public intervention which will involve more decisions by public bodies.
I shall not comment on this; I merely cite it for the record. Perhaps we will take note of it later. I have already spoken of the Freedman report. I believe it is a move in the right direction. I suggest there are many moves which should be made by the department and the minister in order to provide better labour legislation in this country.
Then there is the matter of the winter works program which was mentioned by a previous speaker. I do not believe this program should have been eliminated. What surprised me at the time it was dropped was the fact that when the principle was adopted the members of the Canadian Construction Association and others were not advised. The action taken by the government apparently was unilateral. I believe the winter works program was an excellent one. There was a suggestion by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, I believe, that the vocational and adult training programs had taken the place of the winter works program. I doubt this very much. However, I do not downgrade adult or vocational training because I believe these are excellent programs. I know that in my own area these programs have been a Godsend in respect of training not only the younger but also the older people. I believe that the winter works program should be resumed.
I think my time is about up so I shall hurry along. The other day in the house the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as reported on page 2784 of Hansard, asked the Prime Minister about the rate of unemployment and what steps the government intend-
November 21, 1968

ed to take to combat unemployment in this country. The Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, we had quite lengthy statements on this matter during the budget debate, and we will have a chance to make others on the estimates next week. As you prophesy, I could make a lengthy answer to this question to indicate that this increase in labour force unemployment is due to many factors-
And so on. He said finally:
Actually, Mr. Speaker, I have a lengthy answer here.
Before this debate is over I hope the Prime Minister will enter it to give us this lengthy answer concerning the most pressing problem in this country, that of unemployment.

Members of this party will have other matters to raise. In the meantime I reiterate that I hope the Prime Minister will tell us what he and his government intend to do to combat unemployment in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the Minister of Labour for his masterful, scholarly and practical speech in which he has expressed the labour policy in clear, bold and humanitarian terms. Certainly labour and management today are struggling not only with problems between themselves as immediate parties but also with problems caused by the impact of the age of automation.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Representing as I do the great labour riding of Hamilton-Wentworth, which is largely urban and in which many thousands of our Canadian labour force reside, I am proud to participate in this debate. I am proud because the minister has correctly assessed the importance of automation as a vitally serious problem which requires immediate and continuous action.
I for one will never support the view that labour itself should bear the brunt of technological change. This is a false concept. We must take the initiative in this House of Commons in grappling with these serious problems which have been referred to by the experienced hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He has also on a number of occasions expressed worry and concern about those on fixed pension incomes who have been caught
Supply-Labour
in the inflation squeeze, that dastardly enemy of the Canadian nation.
Surely we cannot stand by and watch capable industrial workers being cast aside as a result of new industrial methods. Industrial workers are not machines; they are an integral part of the company and they must not be cast aside. We must urge management to co-operate more fully, and at greater depth, in planning, as part of their responsibility in respect of integrating the roles of those who are no longer immediately employed in the industrial climate of the day. We cannot deal with unemployment problems simply by carrying out studies, by indifference or by instituting capital cost projects. We cannot take the attitude that cost is a factor which can be considered without dealing with labour and automation. Perhaps the answer is that the government and management must both provide re-employment and retraining for the victims of technological change.
I speak as one who was fortunate enough after the last war to have had the benefit of the Liberal government's retraining program for veterans. This was one of the most magnificent pieces of legislation which ever appeared on the statute books. It is true that this took place after an enormous war and was immense in scope, but it is also true that thousands of young Canadians were integrated in the mainstream of Canadian life by reason of the forward-looking and visionary attitude of the then minister of labour which resulted in this practical legislation. That minister had to deal with a more drawn out and more complex labour structure.
The present Minister of Labour is a hardworking capable man. The legislative background on which he is building was formulated by the late Prime Minister Mackenzie King and carried forward by other ministers such as the late hon. member for Welland, Humphrey Mitchell. That policy was continued by him and by other men of his stature. These men were reinforced by-
Give us the names of some of the others who impressed you so much.
What has been accomplished was not accomplished solely through the work of ministers of labour.
Jot down these names ahead of time. That's a good tip.

Thank you, sir. These men have done their jobs and have gone down in history. This parliament has capable men on

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
both sides of the house. Many of them have far more experience than I. It is my feeling that all members of this house wish to grapple with these problems. We should not turn the other cheek and simply say, let these people eat cake. That is not the attitude of this parliament or the Canadian people.
Another problem of national interest became evident this summer. It resulted from a breakdown in negotiations. When there are strikes the consumer should be regarded as an integral element of negotiations and discussions. Perhaps we have reached the stage when the department of consumer affairs should be represented at least as an observer of what is going on during labour-management discussions. This may be to far-reaching and may strain things too much, but I believe it is a good idea which should be expressed.
National strikes cause tremendous crisis in our economy. They rock the boat to the greatest extent, just like the immediate results of a tempest. The medium of television provides us with a great communications system, and it seems to me there is great merit in having a representative of the consumer affairs department present at the deliberations of labour and management. Such a representative could point out to the labour and management representatives the effect of the positions they were taking on the economy. These men should go to management and point out the effect on our economy of their demands. They might also go to the labour negotiators and indicate the results of their demands for a certain increase in wages. They could show these people how the cost of living would be increased if they continue to hold out for their demands.
I do not hesitate in saying that it seems to me that in the past too much emphasis has been made on labour and how much a man is being paid. We should also consider management and price increases. If we have not the duty, at least we have the moral responsibility to make public the effects of enormous increases in prices. This is true also of the labour aspect of this matter. At this stage I do not advocate a prices review board, but I think we should keep this in mind. We should not shrug our shoulders and say it is completely impossible. This matter should be discussed in this chamber. We should turn our attention to the possibility of an economic prices review board as under the British system. I should like to ask the minister to comment on this.
[Mr. Gibson.1
We should not leave this ship without sails because when the sails go down the ship wallows around in the sea with no certain course. We must consider our economy. For many years the inflationary effect of high wages and high prices has confined the consumer in a straitjacket. We must protect the consumer. The people who elect members of parliament are consumers. Labourers and management staff are consumers.
Before concluding I must not refrain from expressing the view that many problems in labour-management relations are caused by a lack of a humanitarian approach in dealing with employees. This is not a narrow, partisan view. Many companies are progressive and interested in their employees' welfare. On the other hand, many employers are heartless and consider their employees as parts of the plant or fixed machinery. They consider their employees as a number of bodies to be sent here or there. They feel that the company is nothing more than a profit-making machine. These employers should realize their responsibilities in respect of the rights of employees. A great deal of good would result if more presidents of corporations would occasionally drop in at the homes of their workers. Perhaps many of them do. The humanitarian aspect of labour relations has not been fully exploited by management. This government has taken the initiative in this respect. Management should be encouraged to do more and go farther with this approach.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested and pleased to hear the minister say in his speech that as far as he is concerned the just society is one in which a decent standard of living is a right and not a privilege. I am sure we all agree with that. However, I believe we should examine the record of this government since it took office to see what it is doing to bring about that kind of society. We heard during the election campaign a great deal of talk by the Prime Minister about the just society, and all Canadians are interested to see just what the government has in mind regarding its concept of the just society. We want to find out what the government is doing to bring about the kind of just society in which the Minister of Labour says he believes, and in which I am sure we all believe.
I would like to speak for a few minutes about the question of poverty in this country and the minimum wages paid by industries
November 21, 1968

that come under federal or provincial jurisdiction. In August the Economic Council of Canada produced one of its numerous reports. In that report there was a chapter of 37 pages devoted to the subject of poverty in Canada. The economic council tells us that there are in this country no less than 4,200,000 people living in conditions of poverty. We are told also that most of these people are not unemployed and living on welfare but are working for minimal wages. We are told there are no particular areas in which poverty is concentrated, that it is spread all across the country and a great deal of it is found in large cities which are normally considered to be affluent societies.
In its chapter on poverty the Economic Council of Canada says that in the view of its members poverty in this country is no less than a national disgrace. When asked whether he agreed with this assessment, the Prime Minister said he did agree that poverty as it exists today in Canada is a national disgrace. I think every one of us would agree that in the just society we would like to see there is no place for poverty. We who would like to see this kind of just society develop agree that we must leave no step untaken, no stone unturned, to eradicate poverty as much as possible in our country. With this in mind, on September 13 I asked the Prime Minister the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. Since the Prime Minister has stated that he agrees with the finding of the Economic Council of Canada that poverty in Canada is a national disgrace, and since the commission has reported that a great deal of this poverty occurs because people who are working are not receiving sufficient wages to enable them to bring up their families in decency and reasonable comfort, do the Prime Minister and the government intend in the very near future to increase the minimum wage as it applies to industries under federal jurisdiction, particularly as this would be an incentive or an example to the provincial governments?
The Prime Minister replied that the government did not intend to take that kind of action. Therefore I went a little farther and asked the Prime Minister what he intended to do to reduce or eradicate poverty in the just society that he intended to develop in this country. His answer was:
Our attack seeks to ensure that inflation will be curtailed in Canada. We believe this will be the best attack on the problem.
Let us consider what the government has done since the Prime Minister made that statement with regard to curtailing inflation. At the time he spoke, the figures of the
Supply-Labour
Dominion Bureau of Statistics show us that inflation in Canada had increased by 3.6 per cent over the previous 12 months. One month later we are told that inflation in Canada had increased by 3.8 per cent over the previous 12 months. Today we are told that inflation in Canada has increased by 4.2 per cent over the previous 12 months. So we can see that the people of this country, especially those living below the poverty level, are considerably worse off today than they were when the Prime minister gave me that answer in the house two months ago.
This gives hon. members an idea of just what this government is doing to control, remove or eradicate poverty, which we all agree we cannot allow to exist in a society we would call just. The Prime Minister told me on September 13 that the program the government considered to be the best way of dealing with poverty in this country was to curtail inflation. Is inflation being curtailed by this government? It is certainly not. It has increased in two monthly stages in the two months that have passed since the Prime Minister made that statement and outlined the government's policy in this respect. Therefore we can see that not only is the government doing nothing to control or reduce poverty in this country but since the Prime Minister gave me that answer it has become considerably worse and every indication is that it will continue to get worse month by month.
On November 13 I drew this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister. I pointed out that he had told me that the government's program for reducing poverty was to curtail inflation, and that it simply was not working. I asked the Prime Minister whether the government, in view of this fact, had any new plans for dealing with poverty in this country, which the Prime Minister had agreed is no less than a national disgrace. Once again the Prime Minister gave one of his slick answers. He said that of course the answer was in the budget and if we would examine the budget we would see what the government was doing to control inflation. If we examine the budget we see that it contains an increase in taxes over the next year of no less than $845 million. Every member of this house knows that an increase in taxes increases the cost of living because the goods we buy are made more expensive in that the taxes are added to the price of those goods, and the taxes that we pay out of our pockets increase the cost of living. That is inflation.

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
So we can see that next year inflation will continue, probably even more rapidly than it is increasing at the present time. Yet this Prime Minister, who made great speeches on the hustings about the just society which this country was going to have under a Liberal government, has proved that he has no intention of eradicating poverty or of curtailing or controlling inflation, which he said is the government's approach to eradicating poverty.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
So we see that this government refuses to do tf iee things that are necessary to control poverty. The first one is to set an example to the provinces, under whose jurisdiction most industries operate. If this government would increase minimum wages in industries under its jurisdiction, it would set an example to all provincial premiers. The government has refused to do that even though I pointed out to the Prime Minister that the last time minimum wages for industries that come under federal jurisdiction were raised was three years ago and the cost of living has increased 'by no less than 12 per cent since then. Yet the Prime Minister refuses to raise minimum wages and thus to set an example to the provincial governments across this country.
Second, the government has been requested an a number of occasions by myself and others to call together the provincial premiers, having set an example by raising minimum wages for industries under its jurisdiction, to point out the need for them to raise minimum wages for industries under their jurisdiction so that people who are living in poverty because they are working for inadequate minimum wages, in some cases as low as 80 cents an hour, can improve their standard of living. Yet the federal government refuses to do that. I have asked the Prime Minister, when he has all the premiers here to discuss financial and constitutional matters, to ask them to stay perhaps an extra half day to discuss what can be done to eradicate something which he admits is no less than a national disgrace. But he says he will not do it. They will be too busy talking about constitutional matters, all of which are very important but are not as important as taking steps to eradicate poverty among one-fifth of our population. This is the most important problem that can be dealt with today, but the Prime Minister refuses to do it.
The third thing he refuses to do is to curtail inflation. I asked a question today. I produced a quotation from a speech which the secretary of the Treasury Board made to the

Canadian Tax Foundation this week in which he said that this government neglects to examine the need for the programs it is pursuing. I asked the Prime Minister whether, in order to curtail inflation and the tremendous expenditure that is going on in this country, the government would not stop what the secretary of the Treasury Board says is being done. The Prime Minister simply laughed the whole thing off and said that the question dealt with something that had probably happened ten years ago. That is how seriously he took it in spite of the fact, may I point out, that the secretary of the Treasury Board had used the present tense, and if hon. members will read his speech they will see that. He was talking about what is going on now, not five or ten years ago. He told us what the government is doing and what it is not doing, but the Prime Minister is not interested; he could not care less. The Prime Minister talked glibly on the hustings about a just society because he wanted to win votes and to get a Liberal government elected. Now it turns out that what he was talking about was a sham, a farce and a hoax, that he simply talked about something that he had no intention of producing, namely, a just society.
Has the hon. member noticed what has happened to the Gallup poll since the election?

I am telling you about the kind of thing that is going to defeat the government four years from now. You just wait to find out. I take it that all the Liberal members in the house now are proud of the just society-
Hear, hear.
Thank you for the applause. As I said, they are proud of the just society which contains a built in poverty about which the Prime Minister intends to do nothing, as we know because he has said so.
How does the hon. member know?

Because he has told the house so and because he has refused to do the various things we have asked him to do, to raise minimum wages and to curtail inflation. Inflation and poverty are increasing day by day before our very eyes, but you people do not care. You are in for four years. What do you care whether people starve? What do you care about people who live in poverty? What does the Prime Minister care about the fact that people are living in conditions which the Economic Council of Canada appointed by
November 21, 1968

this government describes as a national disgrace? You are proud of that. I hope that the people of Canada will learn from your attitude toward a just society which contains built in poverty that you are not going to do anything to eradicate, to cut back or to reduce poverty.
That is the hon. member's opinion, and he is usually wrong.

Let the minister rise in his place when I sit down and tell me what the government is doing to eradicate poverty. I would also like to hear the Minister of Labour tell us what the government intends to do, but let him do so when I finish speaking. I will be very interested to hear the minister. In the meantime we have been given a further proof that the Prime Minister simply used the slogan "just society" to attract votes in an election. Once he got in he could not care less. He does not know anything about poverty; he has never experienced it.
Oh, oh.

His constituents are the kind of people who do not know anything about poverty. The Prime Minister's answers in the house have shown very clearly that he is not interested in the slightest degree in doing anything to eradicate something which he has agreed is no less than a national disgrace.

[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of my remarks, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) for the courage he showed on at least two occasions in this house, that is recently when he took part in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne and today when he made his statement about his department's estimates.
I want to congratulate him bceause I feel that the position he took with regard to management and labour unions is open, frank, strong and new. I think that too often in the past the politicians and particularly the members of the cabinet have been afraid to state defintie policies.
Before going on to something else, I would like to take this opportunity to thank and congratulate the members of his staff and the officials of his department for the help they give us so graciously and so quickly when we go to them with a problem. I refer
Supply-Labour
in particular to the opportunity I had recently of visiting the various branches of the Department of Labour, and I think that that was very instructive. In fact, it enabled me to see the facilities available to members in the various departments and especially in the field of labour.
Mr. Chairman, before making personal remarks, I would like to refer now to the remarks made earlier this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I was somewhat surprised to hear him criticize the Minister of Labour's intervention this afternoon. He used the word "lecturing" in a way difficult to interpret, but he seemed to insinuate that the minister was preachify-ing. I do not think that is the case. In his statement, the hon. minister merely stated facts and positions.
At this point, I should like to deal with the labour-management committee which should exist in every enterprise.
I, myself, worked in industry from the age of 18. I was able to see the advantages of maintaining harmony in an enterprise through those labour-management committees.
I think Alcan can be mentioned as an example, because it has had only one very short strike in 1941, and another which lasted four months, unfortunately, in 1957. Considering the fact that this company has been established in Canada since 1901 and, in Saguenay since 1925, it can be said that two strikes over a 40-year span, is no abuse, on the part of the workers as well as the union. It also proves that the company understands the nature of its responsibilities. At the very start, it set up a system of consultation within its plants, so that the grievances of the workers could be studied as soon as they were expresed. In fact that, to my mind, is the best way of preventing grievances, which are left pending, from assuming gigantic proportions which cause strikes when the time comes to negotiate collective agreements.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the employees of the Department of Labour and its Minister should intensify, even more if possible, their work with regard to publicity and contacts with the companies, so that labour-management committees might be adopted in all industries. By the way, I should specify that their creation should be required, not "suggested" but "required", in the various government sectors, because if we want to set a good example for private industry, we, in the

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
government, should at least set up those organizations in the various sectors, in the various departments.
If my information is correct, Mr. Chairman, that is not the situation unfortunately. We are far behind with regard to management-labour relations in government departments.
The present system of arbitration has also been mentioned. It is, up to a certain point, the cause of the various conflicts and strikes which we are witnessing. Clearly, the present arbitration system will have to be modified. The minister has taken a categorical stand, saying that the workers cannot be compelled to accept this system, since it would be quite discriminatory to force workers to accept measures which they are not ready to accept.
As for me, I do not think it is a good formula. Indeed, if we compel workers to accept the decision of an arbitration committee, I doubt that, during the course of such a collective agreement, two or three years, there might be a climate favourable to harmony in the company. The worker who will have to go back to work and accept conditions he is not willing to accept, will certainly be a bad and inefficient worker. I think it is preferable to settle the situation and not to establish compulsory arbitration.
I think that among intelligent men, it should be possible to find a system other than the compulsory arbitration. I know that the Woods commission is studying at the present time the various amendments to the statutes and I think that the minister is waiting, like all of us, the publication of this report, so that the statutes may be amended by the house.
In his statement, the minister specifically mentioned that, while waiting for that report, his department has already undertaken the drafting and preparation of new bills or amendments to acts now in force.
This is certainly some preparatory work which it was necessary to do. Once this legislation is drafted-at this stage I appeal to the leader of the government and to all the colleagues of the Minister of Labour-let the minister introduce it to the house as soon as possible because, in my opinion, the labour sector should certainly have a priority. Most of us have been elected by the workers and I think that we should not forget it.
I notice that, at this time when we consider the estimates of the Department of Labour, the attendance is not as large as one could have wished it to be, and I am a little

shocked. I thought that the members would have taken part in greater numbers in the debate concerning the estimates of the Department of Labour, because it gives them an opportunity to express to the members of the government valid opinions and especially to make known the viewpoints of the various groups which they represent in this house and in particular the workers group.

[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)

The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 19, consideration in committee of Bill No.
November 21, 1968

C-103, respecting Atlantic Peat Moss Co. Ltd.-Mr. Breau-Mr. Faulkner in the chair.
On clause 1-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose on Tuesday, November 19, clause 1 was under consideration. Shall the clause carry?

Mr. Chairman, I will not detain the committee since I do not intend to oppose passage of this bill. I say that not because we agree with the arguments of those sponsoring the bill but because, if this measure is passed, certain numbers of people will gain employment.
Anyone with legal training must have wondered why, after a three year period in which notices were sent from the companies' branch to this concern asking it to file returns as was mandatory under the letters patent, this procedure of coming before the house is being followed. Returns were not submitted as requested. That was a breach of the privileges of the original charter. Now the company comes to the house and asks the house to ignore everything that the companies' branch has done.
It is passing strange that a company which has ignored all the notices that have been sent to it should now try to come before this house and obtain permission to do something. Why is it that more lawyers in this house are not curious about this type of operation? On previous occasions we have suggested that the type of procedure envisaged here ought to be carried out in some other forum, possibly before a committee that would deal with private bills and not in the house. We are very much opposed to the idea of private bills being brought before the house in order to do something that could have been done previously in some other way.
As I understand it, the companies' branch is very insistent that companies that are granted letters patent shall adhere, during their lifetimes to the terms of their charters. I am told by a lawyer that this company must have received a great many letters from the federal companies' branch. In fact, the communications probably ought to be measured in feet rather than in individual letters. There would be a great deal of correspondence. Perhaps one or two letters a day might be sent. In any event the companies' branch would have been most insistent that this company adhere to the terms of its letters patent. Therefore the arguments used before the committee by the parliamentary agent simply are not good enough.
Private Bills
It is not enough for the company to say that it was unaware of its obligations because it was concentrating to a large extent on sales. It has duties to perform according to its charter and it must have been aware of the notices that were sent to it. Surely no one could fail to notice all the communications that would be sent to the company's New Brunswick offices.
I suggest that hon. members who wish to do their duty ought to pay close attention to this type of bill which has the effect of undermining the protection to the general public that is provided by legislation. Agencies of government are set up to protect the general public and businesses. This bill tries to circumvent legislation that has been passed.
This company for a period of years was on very shaky financial foundations. It was almost operated by trustees or a firm of advisers that handled administrative problems. The firm of advisers did not have the courtesy of bringing the companies' branch into its confidence and discussing the matter with the branch.
On June 17 and 22 a notification appeared in the Canada Gazette that this company would cease to exist and that the date of the cessation of the charter would be published. We are now to eliminate that move by this bill. Many directives by the companies' branch must have been sent to this company. When a company says in the Canada Gazette that it will cease to exist and then comes before the house with this sort of private bill, surely it is engaging in a novel type of endeavour. Surely hon. members who are interested in the financial community and in the legal aspects of federal charters ought to be much concerned about this matter.
Here all the machinery that has been set up by the government has been unable to convince this firm over a period of years to toe the line. Not only did the company itself ignore the department but apparently the trustees or the people it had hired in Montreal to do its administrative work also ignored the department.

Mr. Chairman, I raise a point of order.
I wish to point out that we do not have a quorum in the house at present.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have a quorum.

Yes, yes.

November 21, 1968
Private Bills
We did not have it a while ago; there were only 17 of us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At the moment we have in excess of 20 hon. members in the committee.

Mr. Chairman, since we almost did not have a quorum it illustrates my point, that hon. members just are not as interested in this as they ought to be. Surely hon. members ought to ascertain for themselves whether any action we are now taking or about to take that will have the effect of side stepping previous legislation poses a danger. After all, members of the financial community are governed by federal legislation and federal charters.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
I call to mind the number of bankruptcies of certain companies that are closely allied to agencies and to which we have granted a federal charter. Unless we provide machinery to demand certain reports and financial statements in keeping with the companies branch directives at an early stage of a company's financial difficulties, then we may well find ourselves exactly in the same position we were in in the case of Prudential. We all remember the recent bankruptcy of Commonwealth Trust. If it had not been for the fact that the insurance branch of the federal government stepped into the picture, and a period of three years had been permitted to elapse, then perhaps some 20 or 30 companies would have gone bankrupt and no money at all would have been netted. I am sure many shareholders across the country will be appreciative of the safeguards provided by provincial and federal legislation and are able to feel much more secure than would otherwise be the case.
In the committee reports, Mr. Chairman, I was disturbed at certain things I read. For example, one member of parliament continually intervened and finally moved a motion the effect of which was to ask the committee not to bother hearing the parliamentary agent explain the difficulties surrounding this company and why no protection had been afforded under the federal charter. The hon. member went on to ask for an assurance in writing from the parliamentary agent. I think this hon. member was derelict in his duty since he did not even listen to the parliamentary agent's explanation of the situation and why we should override legislation designed to prevent this sort of thing happening. While I am sympathetic to this company, Mr. Chair -
IMr. Forest.]
man, I am sure that the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill will agree that we should only override such considerations in exceptional circumstances.
I am reminded of an argument that was used when we used to discuss divorce, namely, that divorce should not be allowed except in the particular case we were discussing. Each case from the province of Quebec was treated as an exception. We are, in effect, treating this case as an exception and saying that the rules should not apply.
I suggest that the assurance that was given to the committee is not worth the paper it is written on. It serves no purpose whatsoever because the parliamentary agent is not responsible to parliament. I am sure that in most cases the parliamentary agent does not even know what his relationship is with parliament. In fact, I suspect some of them have not even paid to the Clerk their $25 parliamentary fee. Therefore I think his word in this case carries very little weight, and his word to the company carries absolutely none.
We must remember that the parliamentary agent gets his information from the company only. I am sure he did not investigate the wishes of the company shareholders. Therefore they are not protected against the action that we are proposing to take, and in most cases I do not think we can provide them with such protection. We are taking away whatever protection the shareholders have by paying no attention to the fact that for three years the companies' branch was trying to get an assurance from the company that it was operating in the best interests of its shareholders.
Many hon. members will say that this is not relevant to the question now before the committee. I realize the hon. member himself is vitally interested in this matter because the situation occurred in his own area. I am also prepared to take his word that it would be a hell of a good thing to give these employees a long period of employment. But we must keep in mind that he is making an exception here in a legal sense in that we are overriding machinery that we have provided to prevent this sort of thing occurring. I hope this does not become a precedent.
Not in your time.

There are some members of this house who will not learn much about the parliamentary system even after four years. It may be that what I say will not be given much consideration, but to those who want to
November 21, 1968

go for supper I say that I shall be here for a period yet.
If it were within my power to do so I would certainly not permit the passage of this type of legislation, and I am sure there are other members of the house who feel the same as I do. I think we are engaging in a dangerous practice in passing this legislation. I do not think we should override legislation that is set up to establish letters of patent, federal charters and so on. We should make sure that the shareholders of companies and others concerned are given protection in cases where such machinery is abused.
The procedure for so doing is fairly simple. All they need do is make a report to the companies' branch. The branch could then ascertain the facts and decide whether the shareholders should be protected. While we are sympathetic to the cause being espoused here, I suggest we are not at all in sympathy with the method being used, which might be considered a doubtful precedent for bailing out of trouble other companies that get into similar difficulty.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, since we
received explanations in French on that bill, we see our way about a bit more clearly, and I agree with the opinion expressed by the member who spoke before me: it may be dangerous sometimes to rush through bills of this type.
I find it somewhat surprising that members of the government party did not forward any explanations, at least to enlighten us. Considering the salaries of parliamentarians and ministers, we must be informed, because according to the explanations given us, it would seem at first sight that the whole idea was to get rid of someone. It is the first thing that comes to mind; this company was seemingly going to be dissolved or it was, once again, a case of camouflaging some ma-nouvres which were not in the best interests of Canada.
So as the previous speaker said earlier, we will allow this bill to be passed, knowing that because of the promise given to the committee, we shall see, at some future time, a treasurer's report and will thus be reassured that we did not pass it with undue haste.
I sincerely believe that members of the opposition are able to prove their outstanding usefulness, and if, later on, in Canada or even in the United States shareholders of this
Private Bills
company feel that their interests are endangered, it would be quite natural for them-as the government party does not appear to give further information, to come and see members of the opposition who could then tell the house what may happen when we pay a bill about which we are left in the dark.
Anyhow, we shall support this bill, as an exception to a rule. However, as the hon. member who spoke earlier mentioned, we should not make a habit of this sort of thing.

I would like to say just a few words, Mr. Chairman. I agree with the hon. member when he requires members of the ruling party who wish to introduce a bill to provide the house with every bit of information desired. The hon. member will however agree with me that the bill has been under the consideration of the Committee on miscellaneous private bills and standing orders and that there has been no pressure whatsoever to rush the proceedings or to conceal anything.
1	have always, together with the witnesses, answered every question. On the motion on second reading, I was here to answer any question that might be put and the hon. member will surely admit there has never been any constraint or any attempt at holding back the truth.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2.

Mr. Chairman, this clause reads:
Within the two months following the adoption of the present act, all returns prescribed by the said Canada Corporations Act, shall have to be filed and received for and in the name of the said company, notwithstanding any stipulation of the said act, or notice to the contrary.
How do we enforce this? What machinery is available to do so if these terms are not fulfilled? I suggest that we leave out clauses 2 and 3 because we do not have any machinery to enforce them, although there may be some justification for clause 3 because it is reinstating the charter under letters patent.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I have to disagree with the hon. member. Clause
2	is inserted to make sure that the returns that were not filed for three years shall be filed within two months. If the company does not file them within two months then the bill is void and the company has lost its charter, and the notices that have been served to the company have automatically been in effect. If the company does not file these returns then it

November 21, 1968
Private Bills
had better not come to see me to pilot another bill. I think it is important that the returns which were not filed for three years be filed within two months.

I am sure that was the intention. If so we should amend the clause to say that if its terms are not adhered to within two months then the bill becomes null and void. Unless we write this into the legislation we have no agency to act on our behalf to see that the terms of the clause are fulfilled. We should write in a penalty making the bill null and void if the said conditions are not lived up to because otherwise we do not have anything to enforce them.

Mr. Chairman, if I understood the sponsor of the bill correctly he said that if the returns are not filed within two months of the bill becoming law then the effect will be that the act will become null and void. If I am correct then, with great respect, I submit that he is entirely wrong. Once parliament passes a law, that is the law.
Clause 1, which we have just considered, says that the various notices that have been given and Gazetted and published pursuant to the Canada Corporations Act shall be deemed never to have had effect for Atlantic Peat Moss Ltd. That is what this bill is doing. It is saying that those particular notices are wiped out and shall be deemed never to have existed.
Clause 3, which we have not reached, talks about the rights, obligations and liabilities incurred since the issuance of the company's letters patent and says that the company shall continue in operation as if it had never been dissolved. There is no requirement here which says that if the company does not meet the requirements set out in clause 2 then the effect of the bill shall be null and void, as advocated by the hon. member for Timiskam-ing. I am sure the sponsor of the bill would agree that the committee could write a penalty type amendment saying that if this requirement is not lived up to then the act shall cease to have force and effect.
In this case parliament is being asked to make an extremely extraordinary decision. We are being asked to say in effect that something did not exist when it in fact existed. We are being asked to use the eraser, to wipe the slate clean, to say that the parliament of Canada says that all the things that happened did not happen.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
All the members who have participated in this debate have thought of this action in
[Mr. Breau.l
terms of being a precedent and of a subsequent parliament harkening back to it and saying: parliament did that and therefore it is all right to do it again. It seems to me that we should write in some penalty provision. I am sure this could be done. I believe there should be something which would indicate that if there was failure to meet the commitment to the parliament of Canada to file certain returns within two months of the adoption of the act, the force of the act should disappear. If the hon. member would agree to that, perhaps we could spend a moment writing an amendment around it.

The hon. gentleman is right when he states that once parliament has passed an act all clauses of the act are also passed. I do not see the necessity to have a penalty. This is merely to protect parliament and engage the committee to file the annual returns of the corporation. Unless they do this the notices will have an effect on the charter of the company. Although I am not a lawyer, this would seem to me to be clear.

Mr. Chairman, we are in agreement on at least one aspect of this; that is, once parliament passes an act it is the law of the land. If that law is silent on a particular point and is silent on the point of a penalty, then how can something cease to exist? The act will still have full force and effect. Perhaps I might read clause 2 in its entirety where it says:
Within two months following the adoption of the present act, all returns prescribed by the said Canada Corporations Act, shall have to be filed and received for and in the name of the said Company, notwithstanding any stipulation of the said act, or notice to the contrary.
The difficult part is where it says, "the said act". I assume this has reference to the Canada Corporations Act since it mentions stipulations of it. The wording is, "any stipulation of the said act, or notice to the contrary".
Although we are not dealing with clause 3, perhaps I might allude to it since I believe it relates to the whole matter we are discussing. It says:
Nothing in the present act shall be construed as depriving or discharging the directors, and shareholders and the company of any right, obligation or liability incurred since issuance of its letters patent and the said company shall continue in operation as if it had never been dissolved.
If clause 3 were to say, "and shall continue in operation as if it had never been dissolved", followed by words such as, "if the returns required to be filed by clause 2 are
November 21, 1968

not required, then the act would cease to have force and effect", what the hon. gentleman says would be correct.
I should like to move-
-that clause 2 be renumbered clause 2 (a) and that a new clause 2 (b) be inserted as follows:
"Failure to comply with the requirements of section 2 (a) will make all sections of this act null and void."
That is what the hon. gentleman has agreed should exist. If it is not spelled out I do not believe it could be interpreted in that way. I put forward the above amendment seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming. I do not think there is any disagreement among the hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Timiskaming, myself, and anybody else, about what parliament should do. It is a matter of ensuring that what we want to do is properly formed in the words of the act and the bill itself. It may be that one could quibble about a sentence or a word or two in the amendment. Perhaps the drafsmanship is not as precise as it would be were it done by one who spends his time drafting legislation. However the facts are there, and if accepted I believe the amendment would probably clear up what the hon. gentleman sponsoring the bill, and others in this house, want to see done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry? [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, were I not convinced that our two colleagues of the New Democratic party are intelligent, I would say they did not understand anything. However, since they are clever, I have come to the conclusion that they want to make some kind of filibuster. There is an old saying: There are none so deaf as those who will not hear.
The clause we are studying is clear, Mr. Chairman, and it seems our friends are muddling up clause 2 and clause 3, which are entirely different.
Clause 2 says:
Within the two months following the adoption of the present act, all returns prescribed by the said Canada Corporation Act, shall have to be filed and received for and in the name of the said Company, notwithstanding any stipulation of the said act, or notice to the contrary.
It is not necessary to be very competent to know that the companies not abiding by the provisions of the Canada Corporations Act- and I am sorry I do not have the clause before me-immediately lose their operation rights. This point is sure.
Private Bills
However, let us imagine that a director of the company wants to resort to this gimmick to have it evade its responsibilities towards its customers or the government or any others. Clause 3 states that under the Canada Corporations Act, even if the said company has not fulfilled all its obligations according to its charter or finds its operations crippled, its responsibilities remain the same.
It seems to me that this is crystal clear, Mr. Chairman, and those who do not understand must deliberately refuse to do so. The amendment suggested is therefore superfluous and unnecessary, since there are already in the Canada Corporations Act provisions for such cases.
Could the member for Trois-Rivieres inform us why he would oppose such an amendment if it is to shed more light on the situation?
Certainly, Mr. Chairman. I am against it because it is absolutely unnecessary. Why repeat something that has already been said in such an important and basic act as the Canada Corporations Act?
Mr. Chairman, I did not raise this by way of a point of order because it is not really that valuable a contribution the hon. member for Three Rivers has just made.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.

I remember that my hon. friend once said that if I said "British Columbia" in this house he would say "Trois Rivieres". I have always said "British Columbia" since then, so I have honoured my part of the agreement.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)

I think if the hon. gentleman will recall the discussion we had about the use of the designation "Columbia-Britannique" he will remember that I suggested to him-and this was when he sat on this side of the house and was only an honorary member of the Liberal party, not a full-fledged member-that if he and his colleagues from the province of Quebec would quit referring to my province as "Columbia-Britanni-que" I would gladly refer to his constituency by the name he gives it. That has not happened. In any event, we had some discussion

November 21, 1968
Private Bills
subsequent to that. I am not knowledgeable in terms oi detailed understanding of linguistics, languages or grammar, but I have discussed this matter with the people who are knowledgeable, and I have been told what the situation is. It has been suggested that in referring to a riding you must use a proper noun, and the name of a constituency falls within that category. The name being a proper noun, it is correct to refer to the constituency in the French language as Trois-Rivieres, as the hon. member does, or in the English language as Three Rivers, and each is correct.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. This has nothing to do with the bill.
The hon. member for Three Rivers, ou Trois-Rivieres, raised a point of order. Surely hon. members on the other side must know what is going on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. It might be in the interests of the committee as a whole if we returned to the amendment, the clause as amended, the clause as it is, or at any rate some part of this bill.

I take it, Mr. Chairman, that there is no point of order as raised by the hon. member for Three Rivers, and I can proceed to deal with the subject under discussion. The hon. member for Three Rivers, ou Trois-Rivieres, whichever you like, said that the amendment before us, as I understood the translation, was part of a systematic obstruction on our part. I presume he meant on my part, as the mover of the amendment, and on the part of the hon. member for Timiskaming, the seconder, and incidentally the drafter of the amendment.
In dealing with this accusation of systematic obstruction, let me point out that before we embarked upon the consideration of this bill, when Mr. Speaker was still in the chair, after a discussion with the parliamentary assistant to the President of the Privy Council, who anticipated the early passage of this bill, I suggested to the house that it make an order to the effect that upon the conclusion of this bill the house should recess for supper. Parliament only makes such an order when there is an expectation that an item under consideration will be concluded before the expiration of the private members hour. I took that step on that basis. The accusation of the hon. member regarding systematic obstruction is an indication to me of his lack of appreciation of the facts of parliamentary life.

The question as to whether this bill will have some validity arose subsequent to a conversation in respect of clause 2. The answer we obtained from the sponsor of the bill, and I forget the name of his constituency, was that if the company did not file its reports within the required time the bill would be null and void. Perhaps I misunderstood him. Will the hon. member clarify this?

Mr. Chairman, what I intended to say was that if clause two of the bill was not complied with by the company it was automatic that the bill would be null and void.
Clause 1 says that the notices given on June 2 and June 17, 1967, and June 22, 1968 in the Canada Gazette by virtue of section 125(12) of the Canada Corporations Act shall be deemed never to have had effect as for the Atlantic Peat Moss Company, "subject to the following sections." This means it is subject to clauses two and three of the bill. As far as I am concerned the amendment is repetitious and that is why I cannot see the necessity for it.
The hon. member for Skeena suggests that if we pass clause 1 it will become law, but it will be the law subject to the other sections. I am not a lawyer, but this is very clear to me. If the company does not fulfil its obligations so far as clause 2 is concerned this bill will be no good and will have no validity.

Mr. Chairman, I am not a lawyer but I think that what will happen as a result of the gazetted notices on the 2nd and 17th of June, 1967 and the 22nd of June, 1968 under the Canada Corporations Act, or a failure to live up to the obligations, is that at some period subsequent to the publication the charter will be revoked. We are not by the amendment wiping out the company, we are simply wiping out the notice required.
I am not in a position to say who drafted this bill, but I suppose it was drafted by a lawyer with little experience in parliamentary procedure. The bill goes on to say in clause 2 that the company must do certain things within a certain period of time. Clause 3 contains an entirely different obligation. What we are suggesting is that if these obligations are not met we reverse the situation and reinstate the obligations in respect of notice. We are suggesting that in that event this obligation should apply. If the amendment moved by the hon. member for Skeena
November 21, 1968

is accepted, and the obligations are not met, this bill will be deemed not to have been passed.
There is nothing in the bill which suggests that the notices required to be published on June 17, 1967 and June 22, 1968 are now in effect. Apparently they have been published and we cannot reverse that. If the company has met the requirements of the Canada Corporations Act it has met these obligations. All we are suggesting is that we waive this notice. In clause 3 we go further and say that we should forget about the whole thing and that it did not happen. We suggest that the personal liability on the part of the directors of the company should apply.
I am prepared to allow this bill to stand in order that the hon. member might consult the legal personnel, but I am of the opinion that we are not asking for anything other than protection, so that if the company again fails to live up to the obligation in respect of notice, appropriate steps can be taken. The company has failed to live up to these obligations for a period of three years. Perhaps the hon. member would like to move another amendment changing the period from two months to perhaps four or five months. We say that if they do not live up to it, this bill does not apply; the requirements of the old charter with regard to notice of termination will apply and there will automatically be a cancellation of the company.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I am not wedded to the idea of two months. I did not write this provision in the bill; the hon. member or his lawyers wrote it in. I have no objection to that provision being changed, but I suggest we have to include some protection in the bill otherwise a long period of time could go by and we would find we had already wiped out the notice, and the only thing the companies branch could do would be to start all over again, unless we do something to wipe out the terms of our amendment.
It sounds to me rather like the situation where a marriage has taken place, a separation is sought and then we wipe out the separation by applying for an annulment. I suggest that if we write in this provision we will eliminate the annulment and get back to the separation again. It seems very simple to me and I do not know why there should be any objection to writing into the bill this very small amount of protection so that the house does not do something that it will regret in the future.
Private Bills

Mr. Speaker, I do not see the necessity for the amendment because it is quite clear, as far as I am concerned, in clause 1 that if the company does not file its return within two months it cannot use the provisions of this bill. But I agree with the hon. member that there is nothing wrong with the amendment, so I am ready to support it.
