speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Lac-Saint-J ean.

Mr. Chairman, before the six o'clock adjournment, I was talking about the arbitration method now used with regard to collective bargaining.
If the situation is so tense today in the field of collective bargaining it is because monopolies have appeared in our industry and that has led to the creation of the labour

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
movement which in turn tends to monopolize things. In fact, the labour unions are becoming more and more powerful and they bring together a very large number of workers in order to countervail the power of private enterprise.
Therefore, I do not think that we should be shocked at the fact that our trade unions merged, that the various groups united, to be in a position to offset the opposing power.
Mr. Chairman, if we want our economy and especially labour relations to operate more smoothly, more progressively, we must amend the present arbitration legislation to make it more functional and likely to bring about solutions to problems facing the various groups, during the negotiations for collective agreements.
Mr. Chairman, one fact remains in all that: the rising prices and salaries. With the inflation spiral, in the end we are worse off than we were at the start.
After checking with a good number of workers and citizens in my riding, I am wondering whether setting up a control board of prices and salaries might not be indicated.
A while ago, a member for Hamilton-Went-worth (Mr. Gibson) mentioned this possibility. I would go even a bit further: I ask that consideration be given to the advisability of setting up a board to control prices and salaries, on a temporary basis, so that we might return to a realistic and reasonable equilibrium in this aspect of our national life. I believe it would be wise to have such a board which could, with other competent people, arbitrate, if you will, prices and salaries in order to adjust the various sectors.
At the present time, you have well-organized groups of workers, strong industries, and they can demand and obtain decent living conditions. Still, between those two groups, you have this mass of Canadian citizens who are crushed, so to speak, between the two powerful blocks facing each other. I feel that we need some control system of prices and salaries, even if it were only on a temporary basis, in order to go back to a reasonable balance.
I wonder whether, starting from this new balance, it might not be advisable to apply same correction to lower prices and salaries so that we might compete on world markets. For instance, there are countries like Japan where the standard of living and salaries are generally fairly low, that manage to compete with the countries in our hemisphere precisely because their prices are lower. I feel this possibility should be looked into.

At the present time, the point which surely concerns the hon. Minister of Labour, is the famous question of unemployment. I wonder whether it might not be well to declare war on unemployment. Let the country be put on a war footing. If Canada were attacked by any opponent from the outside, all its energies, industries and citizens would be mobilized instantly to fight for the country. But the fact that we are tolerating this group of unemployed constitutes, up to a point, an enemy, since our unfortunate brothers take away part of the country's production without directly contributing thereto.
This segment of the population-and I refer here to the recently published report of the Canada Economic Council-represents a rather significant percentage of our people, almost a third, who do not have the same standard of living as their fellow-citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I think all the energies and efforts available in Canada should be mobilized to fight the scourge of unemployment. I believe that Canada cannot afford the luxury of having so many unproductive citizens, so many people who forcibly have a minimum consumption, but who are consumers just the same, while not contributing to the production. I contend that we cannot afford that kind of luxury, particularly when we consider all that remains to be done in this country. It is illogical to hold up that energy, that potential instead of using it to complete what has already been started and also to start new projects.
Furthermore, after reviewing the needs of other countries, we could use our imagination to produce more in a number of other areas and then give part of our production to other nations whose citizens suffer and die by the thousands in some cases.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, in concluding my remarks, I should like to refer to another matter, automation. I mentioned automation in my remarks on the budget. I think it has also been mentioned by the hon. Minister of Labour in his speech. I may therefore rightly raise the subject again.
Automation, mechanization and modem technology must be taken into account. I ask the hon. minister to let us know as soon as possible what legislation he intends to present and in what fields it will be applied. On page 2 of the text of his speech, it is said that that legislation is being prepared. I am anxious

and I think
November 21, 1968

the majority of the members of this house are equally anxious-to see what measures the government, and in particular the Minister of Labour, intend to take so as to correct the situation which affects workers in the whole of Canada.
I want to draw the attention of the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) to a typical example. In the ending of Lac-Saint-Jean, a municipality of 2,000 inhabitants will be affected soon by the closing down of its only plant. The Saint-Raymond Paper, a pulp and paper plant, announced two days ago that it was closing down at the beginning of March. As a result, 200 families will find themselves destitute and we will have to support them through taxes, by giving them social welfare and unemployment insurance benefits. Is that a desirable situation?
Mr. Chairman, that plant had been established 46 years ago and, during the first years, it yielded profits. However, the management forgot to invest money for the development of the factory and today it cannot even survive, because they did not mechanize or modernize their equipment. Today, they are compelled to shut down on account of competition. We have there an example which specifically proves that businesses have no choice; they must develop and modernize their production line.
It is a known fact that workers are laid off due to automation, but we have the proof today that this company must shut down, because it was not improved. It is not 10 or 12 workers who are laid off, as a result of technical progress, but actually 200 family heads. They are laid off, because during the years preceding the shutting down of the plant, no improvement was done to enable it to compete against other plants.
Mr. Chairman, the municipality of Desbiens in the Lac-Saint-Jean area is doomed to become a ghost town, because that is the only plant there. I have submitted the problem to the Minister of Labour, to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) and to the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development. I hope-which I urge them to do-that they will combine their efforts to consider what could be done in co-operation with the provincial government to enable that Desbiens plant to continue its operations.
According to the company's spokesmen, some temporary solution could be applied apparently while waiting for a permanent one, and if the governments stepped in before the plant closed down, I think it would be pos-
Supply-Labour
sible to keep 200 workers on the job, in the hope that, in the meantime, some permanent solution could be found, so that this plant would not only remain in operation but also flourish in order to create more jobs in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area.

Mr. Chairman, lest it go unnoticed, I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members the colourful flowers being worn by hon. members to my right. I hope this is an indication of their flowery outlook on the situation and perhaps an optimism for the future of our Canadian society.
Oh, oh.

This is the first time I have ever received applause from people of that particular political stripe. In all seriousness, before my time runs out I think I should compliment the minister upon his very fine statement this afternoon. We are hoping that statements of the kind that have been made by hon. members this afternoon will be translated into reality in the Canadian nation of today and tomorrow, because I think the portfolio for which the minister has responsibility is going to become more important, not less important, as may be the case in some other areas of the estimates before us.
I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to make a few general remarks. I have been connected with the labour market, contrary to what many members might think, in connection with everything from railroad building to fishing, trapping for the department of mines and resources, and almost every aspect of the labour market. In fact I have had a lot of practical experience in trying to survive in this society of ours, especially in a particular region of Canada.
With Christmas coming on and the winter months setting in across Canada, I wonder how we can take pride in our Canadian nation. I should like to refer to the people in many parts of Canada today, for example in Quebec, northern Ontario and in northern Canada generally, parts of British Columbia and the whole Atlantic region. These people cannot even think in terms of providing food for the winter, let alone the provision of gifts from Santa Claus for their children. They cannot even think of providing adequate shelter, clothing or the necessities of life, not to mention the important necessity of education so that eventually these children can look to

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
the future with a little bit of hope of getting out of the despair in which they presently find themselves.
How can we talk about the affluent society in this Canadian nation, when we realize that in many regions of Canada there is no afflu-ency, but rather a pseudo type of affluency resulting from the fact that people can more easily borrow money than they could a few years ago, and consequently have more debt than they ever had before. If the Minister of Justice were here, I should like to ask him what constitutes a crime in Canada. Of course the Chairman might rule me out of order on that question, because it would be construed as being off the topic of debate. I contend that there is a great crime in the Canadian nation today, and that crime is being committed by most of the big businesses and the various other agencies that have control of the labour market.
The consequences of this crime are low wages, a low standard of living, the high cost of living and unemployment. People in various parts of Canada are being classified as having committed a crime just because they were born in a particular part of Canada. Somebody in Canada, in many cases this government and as I have indicated businesses of various types, construction companies of various types, have elected to classify as a crime the fact that people live in a particular part of Canada. In my opinion this is a fairly serious situation. We have heard quite a bit of conversation about one Canada. This concept originated when I was a much younger man than I am right now, and dates back ten or 12 years. I believe there has been some effort made to turn the concept into a reality.
We heard quite a bit of comment about one Canada during the recent election. Many people in various parts of Canada were given the hope that Canada would become great. I contend that as long as we have the amount of regional disparity that we have in Canada today, we are going to have not two or three Canadas, but 15 or 20 Canadas. Unless this government is prepared to tackle the problem of regional disparity, not only in the Atlantic regions but many other regions of Canada, we are going to have a multiplicity of Canadas. This is the one great fear I have as a young Canadian. In order to fight regional disparity, there has to be provision for stimulating the economy. These stimulants are employment and a just wage structure.

[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
In the few months I have been in Ottawa a great deal of my correspondence has had to do with the low wages that Canadians in this country are paid. That applies not only to the people of my region but to those all across the country. I hope the minister will take note of my remarks and do something to correct this state of affairs. Many of our workmen across Canada are not receiving the minimum wage to which they are justly entitled, by law. Whether people work in industry, construction, for federal or provincial governments indirectly-that is, in projects coming under the jurisdiction of those governments-or in private enterprise, many of them are not receiving a fair and just wage. In other words, our wage earners are not receiving the wage that is theirs legally.
Hon. members have talked a great deal about the minimum wage that is paid to workers across Canada. Failure to pay that minimum wage shakes one's faith in our society. The winter months are approaching and some people in Canada are faced literally with semi-starvation, and all the ills of an environment which would be disgraceful even in poorer parts of the world, let alone in Canada. There are loopholes and clauses in government contracts as a result of which companies take advantage of their workers and pay them less than that to which they are entitled, by law. This makes one wonder about the sort of society we live in.
I will not expand on my remarks. I have already made representations to the minister with regard to specific areas in which Canadian workers are being gypped of their legal right to wages. I hope the minister will use his good offices to bring about an investigation that will rectify some of these things. That this state of affairs exists in Canada is a crime, and I use that word intentionally. Many in Canada do not earn an income which will even remotely give them a decent standard of living.
The hon. member who led off in this debate said that in the Atlantic region over 5 per cent of the people are unemployed. In some parts of Canada such as Newfoundland 20 per cent of the people are unemployed. I have talked to hon. members from Quebec who have indicated to me the serious situation existing in their province at this time.

We are listening to you over here.
November 21, 1968

It is fine for the hon. Liberal member to say he is listening, but it is time someone said what is to be done. Perhaps the hon. member who just interjected might like to stand up and tell us about the problems in his province. Perhaps hon. members from different parts of Canada might like to follow the courage of their convictions and tell us of the problems existing in the parts of the country they represent. For instance, there are grave problems in northern British Columbia as well as in Ontario.
I am proud to stand here as a member of the opposition and talk of problems that affect all Canadians. I am bringing these problems to the government's attention, and I suggest hon. members on the other side of the chamber might do the same. Since other hon. members may wish to make their contribution to the debate and bring the attention of the government to the problems in their respective province, I shall say no more.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, so many speakers this afternoon and this evening have made remarks that were pro-labour and pro-union, and so many speakers have dealt with problems that concern members of trade unions, that I feel I should start my remarks by saying, "Brother Chairman, sisters and brothers". When I look about me, though, I realize I am not in a union hall.
Brother Chairman, I should be less than frank if I did not begin by saying something about the speech this afternoon by Comrade Mackasey. In fact I was quite impressed by the answer the Minister of Labour gave to my question on orders of the day concerning action on the Freedman report. Likewise I was impressed by the fine speech he made when introducing these estimates this afternoon.
The Leader of the Opposition took issue with the Minister of Labour-
As usual.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The
Leader of the Opposition said he thought the minister was lecturing us, lecturing the house and lecturing the public. There was a certain amount of lecturing in the speech but I forgive him for that, for it seems to me that included in his remarks there was a clear indication that he was lecturing his fellow members of the cabinet. If I understood him correctly he was saying to those cabinet colleagues who were here that, so far as he was
Supply-Labour
concerned, the Department of Labour has to move ahead. It must have the permission of the cabinet to bring in legislation to implement the Freedman report, to do something about the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, to do something to step up the enforcement of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and the Canada Labour (Safety) Code. It must do something about discrimination. You know, all told it was a good speech. It was the kind of speech I can imagine the minister making in cabinet and I think he deserves full marks for making it here, out in the open, on the floor of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: thought he was serving notice that he wants his department to be a department of and for labour. He wants the work of his department to result in labour's having a rightful place in this country. In some portions of his speech he dealt in generalities, but in other portions he was specific, and I congratulate him for that and I confess that I congratulate any Liberal, especially any Liberal cabinet minister, with reluctance for every instinct in me tells me it is the wrong thing to do.
You had better beware.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
My
experience in this house is to beware when a Liberal, especially a cabinet minister, makes a promise and tells us something will be done. I do not mean that the promise will never be implemented, but it takes an awfully long time. Some of my colleagues would like me to mention the year 1919; the Liberals do not want me to do that, because some of them were not born then. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman-brother chairman-and I see we are changing brothers in the chair-
Yes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
-despite my instincts that tell me it is wrong, and that I am making a mistake and will regret it, I will say that in light of what the Minister of Labour said this afternoon, I am prepared to give him a chance. I am prepared to give him a reasonable period of time-I will not tell him how long it is-to deliver and come through with some of the things concerning which he spoke so vigorously this afternoon. I have already credited him with having been specific in two or three cases, so let me add to the list of

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
specifics on which the minister must act if he is to carry through with the position that he staked out in his remarks this afternoon.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
It all began today, Mr. Chairman, with his answer to my question about the Freedman report and his report and his further reference to it in his opening remarks on these estimates. As we all know, the philosophy of the Freedman report is especially important to Canadian labour. My colleague the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby has already spelled out the details.
In the main the Freedman report says that workers have just as much stake in their jobs as management has; that workers have rights with respect to their jobs which are not to be sold down the river by management. I was delighted to hear the Minister of Labour say this afternoon that certain recent experiences have persuaded him that it is not good enough just to do what the previous minister of labour did, which was to tell us that the department would take action on the matter. The minister stated clearly that legal legislative steps have to be taken.
A former minister of labour, whose name somebody over there could not remember, used to say that he always said things in a kindly way, so I am going to turn these kindly references to this Minister of Labour into straightforward congratulations if within a reasonable time he has before the house legislation amending the Freedman report.
That would be fine, Mr. Chairman, but the minister cannot stop there. There is also the whole question of amending the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I know that if I remind this minister that his predecessor but one-his penultimate predecessor, the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration-promised on a certain occasion a few years ago that that act would be amended the next year, I need not point out that in fact it was not amended.
The minister will probably tell me that in the meantime the Woods commission has been established and that we are of course waiting for the report of that commission before action is taken on this question. However, Mr. Chairman, the indications are that that report will be received soon, and surely the department itself is thinking about the things the commission is studying. Therefore I suggest that there are improvements affecting the whole process of collective bargaining that need to be made in the legislation.

I trust that the Minister of Labour, who is a man who tries to see all sides of the issue, will be aware of what some of us think were the pitfalls that were put before us last year in what was then Bill No. C-186, and that he will see to it that any amendments he proposes to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act will not have as their possible result the fragmentation of the collective bargaining process in this country.
I am prepared to leave discussion of that legislation at that point, Mr. Chairman, recognizing that we have to receive first of all the Woods report. But let us not have the Woods report lying around for as long as the report on unemployment insurance has been lying around, or have it lie around for as long as we have had the Liberal platform of 1919.
However, Mr. Chairman, let me move on; as I say I am being very helpful to the Minister of Labour. I liked his speech this afternoon and I think I should reciprocate. I am therefore suggesting things that he could do to show that he really meant it when he said that he wanted to make his department one that will serve the working people of this country.
I think it is time he took a good hard look at the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. Time moves fast in this day and age, so let him not tell us that it has been on the books for only a few years, that we must live with it for 10 or 20 years before we change it. I suggest that he take a look in particular at the minimum wage provided in the legislation. Other people have talked about the minimum wage this afternoon but nobody ventured a figure. Even the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings, who wants the minimum wage raised, did not say to what figure it should be raised.
If the Minister of Labour would like to have it, Mr. Chairman, there is a bill of mine in the list of private members public bills that suggests that the minimum figure should be not less than $1.75 an hour. At present it is $1.25 an hour. I am not terribly proud of the figure of $1.75 an hour, but I think it is at least a minimum below which people should not be asked to work under any condition. Even if a person receives the minimum wage of $1.75 an hour, working a 40-hour week for 50 weeks a year, he will still earn only $3,400 a year, which is about at today's poverty line. So where does that leave the present $1.25 minimum wage, particularly in the case of those who do not get work all year round? Therefore, Mr. Chairman, that is one matter
November 21, 1968

on which his own stance this afternoon calls for action.
I would ask him to take a look at the holiday provisions in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. The code still provides for only two weeks holiday a year, after one year employment with the same employer. I urge that in this day and age this period should be lengthened. Again, Mr. Chairman, I point out that I have a modest bill on the order paper that suggests that after three years employment the annual holiday should at least be three weeks a year.
The minister might also look at the question of statutory holidays. When the bill was brought in some years ago it contained provision for seven statutory holidays. We were able to get that bill amended on the floor of the house in committee of the whole so that it provides for eight statutory holidays. I see no reason why there should not be at least nine holidays. I suggest there is really nothing wrong with the principle that there be at least one statutory holiday per month in this country, particularly since it is a cold country and a few days off in the middle of the winter season might be a good idea. Therefore I urge the minister to take a look at that suggestion. However, if I am going too far in suggesting one day a month, 12 days a year, we should at least raise the figure of eight to nine.
The provisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code relating to the 40-hour work week also might be improved. However, in all realism I suppose I would have to admit that the first job is to get the 40-hour week really lived up to.
By the way, Mr. Chairman, I would call upon the Minister of Labour to include in the stance that he has taken a clear indication that he is not going to be led down the garden path by some of his backbenchers. As the minister knows, there are a couple of private members bills on the order paper in the name of Liberal members, one of which seeks to reduce the position of labour so far as collective bargaining in the civil service is concerned. The other would deny the 40-hour work week to certain workers who fall within the federal labour code. So that while the minister is making these forward steps I suggest that he watch he is not knifed in the back by some of the brothers over on that side of the house.
Then I would urge the Minister of Labour to see to it that his department get cracking on the Canada Labour (Safety) Code. He will
Supply-Labour
remember how in a certain session a year or two ago we were pressed by a former minister of labour-the last one-to get this legislation through. We were debating it in committee and taking time to go into its details. The minister of labour pleaded with us to get the legislation through because the government wanted to get things moving. I do not know whether the regulations under the act are in effect even yet. I see the minister shake his head. He should also shake his head in shame, if he had been the minister for very long, but he does not have to do that because he was not. However, he is the minister now. I will give him a little time to deliver the goods, Mr. Chairman, but this is an area where the goods must be delivered.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I think the minister has to go beyond some of the things that have been regarded as his particular area-for example, the matters I have named such as the Freedman report, the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and the two labour codes. He must also be concerned about things such as poverty-yes, pensions-yes, and the concept of the guaranteed annual income. I was glad to hear the Minister of Labour say this afternoon that he felt it was his responsibility to be concerned about the people who are not able to keep up with inflation. Inflation is a word that gets tossed around a lot in this house and in public debate throughout the country. It is said time and time again that governments must somehow stop inflation, and if the government of the day does not, the opposition of the day condemns it out of hand. Then when the two get reversed the same thing happens in reverse.
I quite agree that steps have to be taken to control the rate of inflation. Steps have to be taken in that area, but let us face the fact that if history, especially the history of the past couple of hundred years, is any guide, we are not going to keep prices where they are. Prices and wages in the year 2000 are not going to be what they are today. Price increases and wage increases are going to take place. The role of government, the role of society in this is to see to it that certain people who cannot defend themselves are not hurt because this happens.
Those who have collective bargaining, and those who get the benefit of wage increases because other people do their collective bargaining for them, are able to keep up to some extent with the cost of living and the increased standards of living. But those on

Supply-Labour
fixed incomes, pensioners in particular, do not have any opportunity to do this, and this is where society and where the government has to step in.
The present occupant of the Chair is fully aware of my concern for one particular group of pensioners. But there are other kinds, other groups of pensioners, particularly people on industrial pensions, who face this problem, and I say it has to become the concern of the Minister of Labour that somehow we get built into our pension schemes arrangements for pensions to escalate so that no group in our society is hurt by inflation. I call upon the minister to take on this idea, along with the others about which he must concern himself.
I have made passing reference to the guaranteed annual income concept, which I think has to come. I think some day it will take the place of minimum wage legislation and unemployment insurance. I plead with the Minister of Labour not to confuse the concept of a guaranteed annual income with the guaranteed income supplement that is in effect so far as old age security is concerned. I am sure he knows the vast difference between these two concepts. I am sure he agrees with me that, taking into account the speed with which things are moving, the explosions all around, 20 years from now if all we have achieved is guaranteed supplementary income, then the poverty of retired people is going to be staggering.
The work pattern is going to shift tremendously. Automation is going to produce drastic changes. Instead of our going blind into all this uncertainty and confusion we should plan for it, and should start now to make arrangements for a guaranteed annual income. Some ministers may say that this concerns some other department such as Finance, or Health and Welfare. It is probably a major concern of the whole government, but this is the minister who is responsible for the well being of the working people of this country, and this is the place where the planning should start.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is one other branch of the work of this department about which I should like to say a word. It involves the question of unemployment insurance. This afternoon the minister pointed out that we dealt with these estimates in the standing committee to which they were referred. But they have been referred back to the committee of supply and we have them before us now, and so I want to urge upon the minister

the urgency of the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which have been promised ever since the Gill committee made its report. I am not suggesting they should just be the recommendations made by that committee: There are many improvements and changes that must be made to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
This is the minister who said this afternoon that he is going to make something out of the Department of Labour. This is the minister who so impressed all of us that we feel we are in a union hall tonight. I say it is time for him to see to it that a job is done in amending that act. In the meantime, even before it gets amended, I urge the minister to take a personal interest on the other side of a question which has been given a great deal of publicity, and that is the desire of the Unemployment Insurance Commission to cut down on cases of fraud against the commission and against the fund.
Let it be perfectly clear, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to condone fraud in any way. I do not want to throw any cold water on any efforts to cut down fraudulant practices, but I do suggest that the way the commission is going about this is going to create an impression among a lot of people that there is a lot of chiselling going on, that downright thievery is taking place, with the result that anybody on unemployment insurance may be suspect.
I say quite frankly that I do not like this pamphlet put out in both languages by the Unemployment Insurance Commission titled "Are you really available for work?". Among other things it gives five examples of people who broke the law. They are all anonymous. One is a waitress, another a railway conductor, and the third a stenographer, the fourth a seasonal clerical worker and the last a sales clerk. No doubt they are samples from the files of the commission, but when you put out this kind of literature you create the suspicion that there is a wholesale amount of this type of thing going on.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission admits that the fraud that takes place amounts to only 2 per cent of the total. An editorial in the Toronto Daily Star of November 16 pointed out that the retail industry would count itself lucky if its annual loss through shoplifting was a mere 2 per cent. But there is the other side of the coin. The reason I raise this is because in my experience many people feel they are defrauded

of their right to unemployment insurance because of the extra zeal of some of the department's officials who call people in, after they have been put on benefit, and get them to make the kind of statements which result in their being cut off.
We went into this question in some detail when dealing with the estimates in the standing committee, and so I do not intend to pursue it further at this time. But I do want to point out that in the minister's absence, when he was over at Geneva at I.L.O. meetings, the Prime Minister answered a question of mine on orders of the day in a manner that I found eminently satisfactory, and I hope the Minister of Labour, if he does not already know about it, will see to it the Prime Minister's statement is carried out.
On Wednesday, November 13, as recorded at page 2685 of Hansard I asked:
In view of the announcement that has been made of increased efforts to check abuses with respect to the unemployment insurance fund, will similar efforts be made to protect the rights of those who qualify for unemployment insurance to have their benefits continue without overzealous officials applying the availability clause too severely?
This was the reply of the Prime Minister:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour is now attending I.L.O. meetings in Geneva. I am happy to give to this house the assurance that is demanded by the hon. member.
I did not think I was demanding it. I thought I was just asking for it, but I suppose that is one of our bilingual problems. At any rate there is a clearcut assurance by the Prime Minister that what 1 was requesting would be undertaken.
I hope the Minister of Labour will see to it that steps are taken to make sure the impression is not created that those on unemployment insurance are a bunch of frauds when, after all, the amount of the fraud is only 2 per cent of the total and when there are people-I don't know the percentage, it may be considerably higher than that-who are denied benefits to which they feel they are entitled.
The unemployment insurance fund is there to assist people who are unemployed because there is no employment for them. I hope the fund will be administered with an effort to make sure that it is not abused, but also with an effort to make sure that people get the benefits to which they are entitled.
Now, with respect to the whole question of unemployment, unemployment insurance and so on, I of course come back to the point that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby made in
Supply-Labour
the opening part of his remarks this afternoon, that the chief concern of the department and of the Minister of Labour should not be picking up the pieces when people are unemployed, but should be the initiating of policies that will produce employment.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
That is all our people want-not unemployment insurance, not being forced to work for minimum wages, but an opportunity to work at productive jobs that will provide levels of wages which will enable all of them to take some part in the just society. I have noticed that for the most part the references to the just society are now made from this side of the house. Liberals do not use the phrase very often; it embarrasses them. But the Minister of Labour did this this afternoon and he deserves credit for his courage in doing so. He made it clear that he believes workers and their families have a right to share in this just society.
Now, Mr. Chairman-I mean "brother Chairman"-I say again that I was delighted with the position the minister took this afternoon. If he thinks I am being friendly and congratulatory toward him now, fine; I am. But if he does not deliver he knows what will happen.

I always get confused about ridings. The hon. member has made me a little inarticulate for a moment. If he finds it strange to say anything complimentary about a Liberal cabinet member, I think my record in the house would show I find it equally difficult to find anything nice to say about the many socialist reactionaries in the New Democratic party at whom I have looked with so much affection for the past five years. I believe however, we do share one thing in common; that is, a deep concern for people, Canadians in all walks of life, entitled to a just society. We differ only with regard to the method by which we would achieve this just society. I often think that their philosophy is better suited to the nineteenth century and, although it is Utopian in concept, as an ideal it is not practical. I believe those of us on this side of the house will attain the just society and at the same time retain the better features of the private enterprise system which has been a character of Canada and Canadians.

I believe I do appreciate the concern expressed this evening by the hon. member from Winnipeg, who has a bill on the order paper for every situation. He suggested that I refer to the private members hour and private members bills for guidance. I will admit there are bills in his name in respect of perhaps every subject under the sun, but they are always progressive in the field of social welfare. They are designed to improve the plight of senior citizens and the position of the fixed incomes of civil servants with lower than standard salaries and lower than standard pensions, pensions which were set on an actuarial system which is long out of date. I have no quarrel with his concept.
I believe most people in this house know that if I am unable as Minister of Labour to implement some of these reforms-not necessarily along the lines the hon. member thinks are appropriate-and unless I am able to find support for this type of reform inside the Liberal cabinet, I would find it necessary to resign from the cabinet and demote myself to the back benches, where I would be free to express my opinions. However, I have confidence in the Liberal government. It has placed on the statute books of Canada every meaningful piece of pro-labour legislation that Canadians deserve and appreciate.
I have very little reservation about my ability to sell my concept to the cabinet, particularly when among the members of the cabinet are such very wonderful Canadians as my colleague who will be charged with the responsibility of eliminating regional disparity in a country as vast as Canada. I would commend to all members of the house the speech the hon. gentleman made in Montreal last night, which was published in great detail in La Presse, because I think it is very thought provoking and very tangible evidence of the fact that we do intend to attack poverty in this country on a meaningful basis.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would hardly expect me to comment on all the pieces of legislation he mentioned. He did mention the Industrial Disputes and Investigation Act. I have prepared no less than 80 some potential amendments to that act, but I am very conscious of the fact that the task force may come forward with better solutions.
The hon. member also mentioned Bill No. C-186. I would hope, when and if this type of legislation is brought forward, that he and other members of the house would approach it objectively and not as a matter of Quebec
[Mr. Mackasey.l
against Canada, the French against the English, or Jean Marchand against somebody else. This is not the type of attitude that makes the committee system in this house more desirable. I am not directing these remarks to the hon. gentleman, because he did not do this. I am referring to some of the people who did appear before that committee representing the labour movement in this country. They did mention to me, in secret however, that even if the bill was imperfect in their opinion and if freedom of association was not as important as national bargaining units, at least they agreed they might have attacked the bill for its weakness in structure and not resorted to an emotional attack on the government in order to defeat the bill.
Many people have been complimentary in their remarks this afternoon. This has a sobering effect on me and makes me more responsible just when I was preparing to rear back and remind the members of the New Democratic party of the failures in Saskatchewan and so on. I should like to comment on some of the issues which have been brought forward and say that I appreciated the remarks of the hon. gentleman opposite from Central Nova, who is the official labour critic of the Conservative party. In the years I have been in this house I have found that he is very strong in debate, and I have no illusions about whether or not he will make it difficult for me on the right or wrong occasion, as the case may be, depending where you sit.
I did appreciate his endorsation this afternoon of the philosophy contained in the Freedman report. I suspect this is the first time a Conservative member of parliament has ever endorsed the philosophy of the Freedman report. I think this is a sign of progress on their part. I should like to attribute that progress to the hon. gentleman, the very genial labour critic from Central Nova. When I take this concept to the cabinet and bring it back to the House of Commons in bill form, in view of the fact that the New Democratic party supports the idea and the official labour critic of the Conservative party is wedded to the philosophy in the Freedman report, the bill should have speedy passage.
The hon. member also mentioned the postal strike, although this more appropriately comes under Treasury Board rather than the Department of Labour. He made the point that much of the cause of labour strikes is not directly applicable to dollars and cents but rather to daily differences between management and labour, differences that grow out of all proportion, so that when the two parties

meet at the bargaining table there is real animosity, which is unnecessary and which prevents management and labour looking after the small details, which are small in their eyes but important in the eyes of the individual worker with a lunch pail. So I compliment the hon. member for bringing this to our attention. I was glad the right hon. Leader of the Opposition was here when the hon. member from Newfoundland-I believe he represents Gander-Twillingate-spoke, because in the very short period of time this young man has been in the house he has proved to be one of the more eloquent members. I should like also to thank the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) for his interesting remarks on the activities of my department.
I appreciate the comments which were inspired to him by his activities in the labour movement. His practical experience as a member and as a worker in our Canadian society give weight to his remarks. I can assure him that they will be considered and that his suggestions with regard to unemployment insurance for instance will be studied,

even though consideration of the estimates of the commission has already been completed.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, who represents one of the really great industrial centres of this country, also impressed me, and I learned much from his contribution, particularly when he spoke quite eloquently and factually about the problems of residual rights and how this is handled in other countries such as the United States, Sweden and England. This really is the basis of the philosophy of Freedman, as the hon. member and I both realize. The hon. member also mentioned the unemployment figures and asked whether I could bring him this evening a projection of unemployment for the winter in Canada. I am sorry to say that I cannot, because this particular responsibility falls under the jurisdiction of the department of manpower in conjunction with the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. I understand the implication of his request and his remarks. Any rate of unemployment is undesirable in a country which should be as prosperous as ours.
I think the departments of manpower, labour and what I have referred to, perhaps prematurely, as regional disparity, should work closer together to attack this problem of unemployment on a permanent basis. There has been reference to the winter works program, but we must realize that this program, desirable as it might have been ten years ago, has done little in a permanent way to re-educate and retrain people who are chronically out of work during the long winter months, which exist in many parts of this country. I think we must realize that the money we spend on retraining these people is a much better investment than simply handing them a shovel during a snowstorm, or asking them to turn over roads and ditches for sewers in the dead of winter under the pretext that this is a suitable winter program.
If we are going to fight poverty and unemployment we have to end this type of program, and spend the money in areas where, in the long run, it will be more meaningful and beneficial to Canadians. Many members have touched on the need for education. Experts from the economic council have told me that a recent study they have undertaken on the mobility of the Canadian work force indicates, that it is much more mobile than we anticipated or realized, and this includes workers from the province of Quebec. There

Supply-Labour
is a direct relationship between education and mobility, and the educated and trained worker is quite prepared to move from certain areas of the country to other areas where jobs are more plentiful.
If we are to reach the type of utopia which I think is within the grasp of countries such as ours we must tie in the whole problem of unemployment and poverty with the problems of education. Some time ago we realized that no one is too old to be retrained or educated. This is one of the areas of priority in the fight against poverty in this country.
Having said these things, and I feel rather deeply about them, I realize that while I may be speaking in a rather non-partisan manner, this is a problem that cannot be tackled by one, two, three or four ministers. This is a problem which must be tackled by all levels of government and all Canadians who have a social conscience. The sooner we reach this concept in . Canada the sooner we will reach that standard of living which Sweden enjoys and which Japan is rapidly reaching, where co-operation and concern for each other is almost a religion. I think these ambitions and desires are not beyond the scope of this government or this House of Commons.
I was impressed as well by the sincerity of the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth who represents one of the more affluent sections of Hamilton. If he were politically partisan I am sure he would say nothing that was pro-labour. He talked about a wages and prices board. Perhaps I should correct that by referring to and talking about an income and price board. When we talk about wages we are again talking exclusively about the worker. When we refer to control we should think in terms of controlling "income", because that is the proper terminology. Income includes the income of doctors who increase their charge by 20 per cent or 25 per cent when called out in the dead of night for instance. It is "income" that properly describes the income of the lawyers, many of whom are in this house, that can stand scrutiny.
All of us who come here to the political table, and all those union members who have power and strength have a responsibility to our fellow Canadians. That is a responsibility not only of the government but also of management and labour.

which he found it necessary to lecture the hon. member for Verdun. I am starting to develop a real affection for that hon. gentleman, and this frightens me. This is not part of my character. Sock it to him.

other hand there is some consolation in the fact that we are able to employ 270,000 more people who are coming into the labour force.

May I ask the minister a question? A few minutes ago an hon. member asked for some statistics on unemployment and I think the minister indicated he could not give them because this was not under his jurisdiction and he did not have the figures. Perhaps in his commentary he could indicate what particular statistics were being sought at the time.

I would be glad to remind the hon. gentleman of precisely what I said. Perhaps he did not hear the question, which was put quite properly. I was asked whether I could give a prediction concerning the rate of unemployment this coming winter in the major cities of Canada. I said I could not because this was not the role of the Department of Labour, and the question would have to be asked when we come to the estimates of the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
Mr. Chairman, the question was-
Mr. Chairman, I should like to finish what I was saying. The hon. member is in bad company.
If you can't stand the heat you had better get out of the kitchen.

I was going to say that the figures I am reading are factual. I got them out of the parliamentary library, and I am sure the hon. gentleman could easily do the same. As to the figures concerning unemployment in the coming winter, I cannot produce them, and this is an honest answer.
I appreciate the quiet, the attention and respect with which my remarks have been treated by the opposition. Obviously people can see that my big problem is to act with the dignity which a minister is supposed to act in a debate, and at the same time I find myself periodically reverting to the role I had before I was elevated to the cabinet. This is a house of debate and I should hope that in the repartee and exchange I have hurt nobody's feelings-certainly mine were not hurt. I just happen to think that in the last election the people of Canada indicated more confidence in this great young man, the Prime Minister, who is going to lead this country toward a just society than in hon. gentlemen opposite. I think his record is excellent. I am sure his
Supply-Labour
concern for the people of Canada, for the working class and for the underprivileged, his direct connection in the past with unions, their causes and their plight, and his willingness to fight for them in court as well as with the strength of his pen, indicates that we have a Prime Minister who is really concerned about and sincerely interested in establishing a just society. I believe that with the complete co-operation of the opposition, that just society will be arrived at much sooner than most people think.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Chairman, thank you for all the applause.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. The reason I want to ask a question is that when I was speaking the Minister of Labour assured me, as I understood it, that he would be ready to advise the house as to what steps the government is taking to eliminate poverty from this country, so far as it can.
Mr. Chairman, I think we should hear from someone else who has something constructive to add.
Than I take it that the minister has nothing to say-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

-and nothing to explain as to what this government is doing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

He has nothing to offer.
I have a brief question, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair has recognized the hon. member for Temiscamingue.

Mr. Chairman, after hearing the hon. members who took part in the debate on the estimates of the Department of Labour, everyone will agree that the regional disparities mentioned in most speeches are strangely alike throughout Canada.
If you listen to an hon. member from the Maritimes, you will hear about economic difficulties with regard to coal mines, the

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
development of natural resources, etc. The same situation prevails in northern Quebec.
I heard a little earlier the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard) talk about Desbiens where something could be done. The problem was submitted to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) and to the cabinet, but it has not been solved yet. Incidentally, I think that the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean, who was previously sitting on this side of the house as a Credi-tiste member, realizes that occupying a seat on the government side does not improve the standard of living of his electors, nor that of Quebecers or Canadians as a whole.
Therefore, he should have remained with us to pursue a more efficient flight.
Mr. Chairman, the situation is the same in other areas. In my own area, people complain that mines have to close down. In the Quebec area, they complain about the shipyards of Lauzon; in the eastern townships, they complain about problems facing the shoe industry and the precarious situation of the textile industry. There are economic difficulties everywhere.
Regional disparities resemble each other very much from an economic point of view.
I limited myself to Quebec, but the situation is the same in Ontario. We also hear the members from the west complain about a lack of industries, and especially those from Manitoba who complain that the overhaul base of Air Canada will be transferred to Montreal. Mr. Chairman, that stirs up a storm in the house. The members from Manitoba complain because hundreds of employees will have to move to another province if they want to continue working.
We have the same thing in the western provinces. In British Columbia people complain about that situation. In the fishing industry, for instance, in business, in the lumber industry, one runs into economic difficulties called regional disparities.
Mr. Chairman, all those regional disparities are related to a single problem: the Canadian economic problem. That is why, following the June 25 election, the future Minister of Regional Development stated categorically on television that, at all cost, the government would have to make a comprehensive study of what economic reforms should be made in Canada. This is the case not only in our region, but all over Canada.
It should be borne in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the minister was speaking about winter

works being replaced by retraining courses with a view to giving more education to our people, our unemployed and our younger people, which will enable them to acquire knowledge that will eventually assist them in finding employment. But the fact remains that, after studies lasting up to three years, depending on the retraining courses, they are not in a better position to find jobs.
The unemployed who are over 50 are not eligible to go to those schools as they are considered too old. What measures can be taken to assist these people?
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
At this very moment, Mr. Chairman, there are over 80,000 unemployed in Montreal alone which is equivalent to practically one quarter of the unemployed in Canada. To these people will be suggested that they register for retraining during the winter. In fact, the present system consists in having the uneducated unemployed become educated unemployed. When people have finished their 10th, 11th and even 12th grade, they are told: "We do not have any work".
In the meantime, the Minister of Labour is at grips with management on the one hand and workers on the other hand. In addition to that situation which affects the labour world everywhere in Canada, and more particularly in Quebec, the minister has to face arguments of ah kinds, right and left. We hear about strikes, the postmen's strike, the longshoremen's strike, the teachers' strike, the students' strike. Why do these strikes exist?
When somebody finally proves to me that in Canada a strike has solved a labour problem then I will believe in the efficiency of the strike. But all the strikes which I have witnessed in Canada were settled by some agreement, which formed the basis of the next strike on expiry of the collective agreement. It has always been the same thing.
I see the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development who was, I think president of the C.N.T.U. nineteen years ago, during that famous strike called the Asbestos "greve de la matraque". Twenty years later, are the workers treated any better? Let us go to Asbestos and see, let us talk to the workers in Asbestos. Blood was running in the streets. Did it change the system? This is why I find it indecent for some workers to rouse other workers against management, when these leaders should act as peace-makers between labour and management. They should be goodwill ambassadors, not distributors of boxing gloves or fomenters of hate. The workers
November 21, 1968

need the employers just as the employers need the workers.
I heard earlier the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggest his famous solution. He always asks for the same thing: a minimum wage of $1.75 an hour and seven days of leave with pay. He would prefer eight or nine days of leave with pay; he would not object to one day a month which would mean 12 days of paid holidays and shorter working week. They feel sure that this is the answer. There are people working in small restaurants, for instance, who earn $30 or $35 a week. Try to pay them $1.75 an hour, and the boss or the little restaurant owner will end up bankrupt. We know that some industries cannot pay that kind of wage, because as soon as the wages would go up, it would trigger an increase in the cost of living. In fact, salaries go into the cost price of goods and services. This is what people do not understand. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is completely at sea. If we increase salaries, up go the prices; but reduce the working hours and then increase productivity, nobody can make head or tails of that.
A Chinese might understand the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but no Canadian would.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, when I was listening to the hon. member's speech I was reminded of the late Clement Attlee and of his speeches of 20 years ago, as well as of the speeches of the Right Honourable Harold Wilson, Prime Minister of England, when both gentlemen sat on the opposition benches. But, when they came into power, they did exactly the opposite of what they had been preaching.
To realize that, let us take the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to England tomorrow morning, to show him at close range the magnificent achievements of State socialism, in England, in every field. Financially, Mr. Chairman, England has gone to the dogs. Why? Because of a mad system similar to our own. The Liberals agree with me. They know that our system is wacky. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration and the Minister of Labour know it.
A gang of madmen.

Yes, and some people go a little further, they say we are ruled by the most outstanding of those madmen. What are we to do?
Supply-Labour
Mr. Chairman, the day after the election I was listening to the comments of two union leaders, Mr. Marcel Pepin, president of the C.N.T.U. and Mr. Louis Laberge, president of the F.T.Q. They stated that all those who had voted against the New Democratic Party were idiots. What did Mr. Louis Laberge ask before the elections? He asked the workers of Quebec to vote for the New Democratic Party but they did not listen to him, because they did not take him seriously. We saw Mr. Marcel Pepin, on television on election night; we often see him there. He looks like a regular guardian angel; he is a mealy-mouthed type, and is as quiet as they come. He reminds me of a monkey that would have escaped from the Granby zoo, or something like that. And what is his program? Stir up the workers against the employers, nothing else. A distributor of boxing gloves.
Mr. Chairman, in every socialist country throughout the world, when the government fell into the hands of union leaders trouble began. I know that from experience. I have been in Russia, in Czechoslovakia and in other socialist countries. Go to England and you will see the same thing. Those at the helm are former union leaders who used to say that power should belong to the workers. Theoretically it does belong to them now, but all they get is a kick in the pants, because they are not the real rulers.
Recently, in Czechoslovakia, students had led the country on the road to socialism. Now, the people are trying to get rid of it but they cannot since the U.S.S.R. who is practically next door, keeps them under her thumb and they can neither budge, move forward, nor shake themselves free. Such are, Mr. Chairman, the advantages of socialism.
On the day when people like Messrs. Marcel Pepin and Louis Laberge have any political power, we will witness here the same things that are happening now in England.
There is no need to go that far. In our own country, Canada, did not the New Democratic party, successor to the C.C.F. party, hold office in Saskatchewan during 17 years? With what results? It is the only province from which the people migrated to the other provinces. They went to work in Alberta and British Columbia to pay Saskatchewan's socialist taxes. In fact, there was no work to be had in that province.
And that is not the worst, Mr. Chairman. The provinces of Manitoba and Alberta spent millions of dollars to prevent rats from Saskatchewan from eating up their crops. These

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
are not tales, but tacts. I do not lie; it is the gospel truth.
This being so, would we let men like Mr. Pepin and Mr. Laberge guide us and direct us towards that type of system?
Mr. Chairman, I am not against unions, far from it. I am entirely in favour of trade unions but only those where workers control their own business and are not told what to do, as if they were children. That is exactly what is happening now.
When Mr. Laberge asked Quebeckers to vote for the New Democratic party, did they comply? Let us not be funny! They would rather vote for my hon. friend, the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
In the city of Montreal, that party spared no effort. They were quite sure they would take about ten ridings. But they did not win a single one. So much the better! However, they have the comfort of knowing that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) once belonged to their group. The hon. Minister of Forestry and Rural Development at one time was flirting with them. The hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) had connections with them for many years. Therefore, the members of the New Democratic party feel a little bit at ease with the present government or, at least, with the leaders of the present government.
All this, Mr. Chairman, to say that we must make some improvement. I am all for respecting labour unions. But let us first of all respect the workers. That workers should unite to study together those problems they have in common, I agree with that. I am also in favour of discussions between management and labour. But whenever a labour leader raises an almost unsurmountable barrier between the workers and the management, he is then abusing his authority. He is not upholding and serving the best interests of the Canadian workers, because employers as well as workers are human beings.
It is possible for these people to discuss. I am myself an employer. There was a strike in my establishment. What did it settle? Nothing, like I said at the beginning of my remarks.
I have yet to see a strike that will settle labour problems. In Quebec, some strikes have been going on for a long time. What will they achieve? Employees of the Quebec Liquor Control Board have been on strike for five months. What does it amount to? For
[Mr. Caouette.i
the first few weeks, it is great. You are ready for anything. At the end of five months, Mr. Chairman, if the employee does not realize the situation, go and see his wife and children; they realize it. And yet when these workers go back to work, they will find no great improvement in their working conditions. However, they will have gone into debt for perhaps five or ten years and will have to go to finance companies and ask for credit at the corner store and everywhere in order to manage and make ends meet; but they will not be able to.
Mr. Chairman, problems are not solved by strikes. When my colleague the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) spoke of labour matters this afternoon, he knew what he was talking about, because he is a former union president. He did not organize strikes, but he was the leader of a group of hard workers and, at the same time, he met with management in order to act as liaison between the two groups and bring about an understanding. I think in this respect he could give a few very useful lessons to union leaders today. Even my hon. friend the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development should have known the hon. member for Kamouraska twenty years ago; he would never have had anything to do with the Asbestos strike.
Mr. Chairman, I do not say that all present union leaders are wrong. However, most of them, the ones we constantly see on television, are always against everything. I sometimes wonder what prevents them, since we live in a free country, from setting up industries, a steel mill, for example, from becoming employers and treating their employees according to the views they now express or as they say workers should be treated. What is preventing them from setting up companies and becoming employers? But that is not what they are looking for.
Instead of trying to create something, they try to demolish, to destroy what others have built. They tell the employers what to do; they always talk on behalf of 125,000, 132,000 or 134,000 members and they are sure of them because on television at least they have real power. Then there are politicians who are afraid. Mr. Chairman, you would not believe it. They are afraid to lose votes, they are afraid to lose elections. That is why today there are so many abuses in the field of labour and management relations; it is because politicians do not have the courage to assume their responsibilities. The politicians were afraid when they should have
November 21, 1968

stood firm, when they should have stated the facts, when they should have been frank with the population, the workers, the lumbermen, the people as a whole. If they had done all that, there would be fewer strikes today.
In the field of labour in Quebec, people blame the students because they stage sit ins, they argue, they occupy buildings. It must be noted, Mr. Chairman-I call the Prime Minister's attention to that-that their own professors showed them the way two or three years ago when they attacked the school board, held demonstrations against the provincial government or against the administration of this college or that university. You set a bad example and then you blame the students for following it.
The parents who deplore such things are in the same situation. The Liquor Control Board employees are on strike, and there was a strike of postal employees! During the latter strike, there were threats against the Prime Minister, the government, and then the Canadian public to deprive them of the postal service as long as they felt like it. The strike has been settled, but who pays for it? The workers who went on strike gained something. But today, it is the public in general that is paying for the increased postage stamp prices, for the transportation cost of the mail. It is paying a rather a heavy price for the postal employees as well as the famous strike of the Montreal dockers.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
This does not mean, Mr. Chairman, that longshoremen, postal employees and so on do not deserve a better income-I do not say an increased salary but an increased income. As long as we continue to increase income merely through salary increases which are part of the cost of goods, we shall always face the same problems. We shall be running in a circle, struggling in a strait jacket. And what are the Creditistes suggesting? They suggest to increase the income, but in such a way that the increase will not be a part of the cost of goods. And how can we achieve this?
Let us not study my statistics but those of the federal government which indicate that this year the national production of the Canadian labour force amounted to $67 billion. The total income of the members, the salary of my friend, the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, my salary, the profits of all the business people in Canada, and all the other incomes put together, will amount to $48 billion. The government then warns us
Supply-Labour
by saying: Productivity will increase by about 5 or 6 per cent per year and therefore the salaries must not be increased by more than 5 or 6 per cent.
Let us say, for example, that our production will amount to $70 billion next year. With a yearly increase of 6 per cent, that would mean a production of $74,200 million. It is an increase of $4,200 million of new production, and there is no need of increasing our income by more than 6 per cent a year. Let us say, for example, that our revenues amount to $50 billion; with a 6 per cent increase, that means $3 billion. How can we, Mr. Chairman, purchase $4,200 million of new production with $3 billion of new income? That is the problem. So we say that the difference between the two can be used to increase the income of all Canadian citizens, without that coming into the prices. We are right, and the minister knows it.
According to the facts, there is now a difference of $20 billion with regard to the economic operations of 1967-68 alone. For $20 billion of production, there is no corresponding purchasing power, and $48 billion is purchased with the national revenue. This $20 billion production is not sold because we do not have the revenue to purchase it. What does that mean? Mr. Chairman, the Bank of Canada could create, in figures, about $1,000 per capita if the government of Canada gave the order to do so and to distribute the money to every Canadian citizen, without creating inflation, without this being included in the costs of goods, without increasing the cost of services. Then, we would achieve an economic balance which would give citizens a purchasing power enabling them to purchase products which exist.
We do not know what to do with our products, and the unemployed in Montreal need them. Why can they not buy them? For lack of purchasing power. The minister knows that. The number of our unemployed will increase because of automation. What is the government's solution in the face of automation? No solution. So, unemployment takes over. But what do we advocate?
In so far as machines, automation, science, progress and knowledge are being used to speed up production and to replace man at work, let us establish a system thanks to which Canadian men, women and children will have an income that will allow them to buy the products of automation, and of machines. This is not inflation. This is balance, common sense and logic.

November 21, 1968
Supply-Labour
The 86,000 unemployed of Montreal who earned maybe $100, $125, $130 a week, while to-day they get only $30, $33 or $36 as unemployment benefits, are out of work. Why? Because there is a superabundance of products and the factories no longer need their workers. When there is overproduction, factories close down. If it is true that the unemployed is laid off because of overproduction, why is he not given precisely the salary he used to earn when he was at work? Indeed, let us pay him his salary until he finds a job. Products are there, and he only needs purchasing power.
The government does not consider that possibility. It thinks in terms of retraining of manpower and we are back again in the same system, going round and round, without ever finding a way out. It has been suggested that there is one, because the minister was speaking a while ago of the just society. It is all very well to speak of a just society! But in the meanwhile, there are 28,000 families in Montreal on welfare and 86,000 people who draw unemployment insurance. What does it represent? It represents a population of
150.000	to 200,000 persons. Now, if 300,000 or
400.000	persons out of a population of 2 million in the City of Montreal do not have a sufficient purchasing power to buy the necessary products for their subsistence, Mr. Chairman, where are we going with the government of the just society?
That is why we have all these clashes, and they are going to become much more frequent. In fact, we are building a tower of Babel. The only difference with the real Tower of Babel, is that when the people at that time realized that there was confusion, that they could not communicate with or understand one another, they gave up; but we are too stupid, and we go on with the work. It is the only difference.
Mr. Chairman, the problem can be solved. The root of the evil is not in the minister's heart, nor in the heart of the government; Finance is the villain. Let us first put Finance at the service of Canadians. It is up to the government to take it upon itself.

May I thank you, Mr. Chairman, and the members of the committee for allowing me one minute in which to make my maiden speech in this house. We have heard speeches from members of the opposition dealing with unemployment, the elimination of poverty and regional development, but in some manner they seem to place responsibility for these immense problems on the

Minister of Labour. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not appreciate the relationship that these problems have to the minister's department. However, I wish to advise the committee of some important problems that do have direct relationship to the minister, and which may properly be recognized as such by some of the members who have done much of the complaining here today.
Hon. members, as I say, have talked about unemployment, regional disparity and the elimination of poverty. In my constituency, Mr. Chairman, there is a great deal of industrial development. Several areas are exporting coal to Japanese markets, markets that we hope to exploit in the near future. However it disturbs me to see that in these areas there is an insufficient supply of labour.
At the same time, Mr. Chairman, I listen to members in this house saying that in other parts of the country people are unemployed. Last week the manager of one of the coal mines in my constituency visited me in Ottawa and told me that he could ship twice as much coal to Japan as he is now shipping if only he had enough labour to bring up the coal from under the ground. This man, Mr. Chairman, is prepared to provide the cost of moving workers from where they presently reside to his area in western Alberta. He is prepared to retrain them to equip them with the skills necessary to engage in the occupation of mining this coal. He is also prepared to provide assistance in the matter of obtaining housing for these workers. Yet as I say, Mr. Chairman, hon. members from other parts of Canada tell us that there is insufficient work in their constituencies.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
