speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall have to be quick about it because I have only seven minutes to deal with a fairly important matter. On November 7, I put a question to the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), asking him to explain to us why the C.B.C. had allotted only an hour and 37 minutes to the Ralliement credi-tiste at the time of its last convention at Sherbrooke, while allotting that same weekend, eight hours and 46 minutes to the Parti quebecois.
Later, several similar questions were put to the minister in this house.
It should be noted that the minister attempted twice to shirk his responsibility and to tell the house who is responsible for the C.B.C.
The same thing happened when, on November 7, the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), put a question to him asking when he intended to set a policy with regard to the allotment of the time on C.B.C. The hon. Secretary of State then told us, in this house, that the C.B.C. was not answerable to the Secretary of State but instead to Parliament. The following day, on November 8, the hon. member for Lotbiniere, further to his first question, asked the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who is responsible for the C.B.C., whether it is Parliament or the Secretary of State?
The Prime Minister replied, as seen on page 2572:
Mr. Speaker, this is a question for the Secretary of State.
Now, it is obvious that the C.B.C. seems to be answerable neither to Parliament nor to the Secretary of State. It seems to act as it sees fit. Indeed, on many occasions- I have proof of this-it has been prodigal with the Liberal party. Besides I have figures here on the allotment of time slots to prove my statement.
The C.B.C. has no definite policy with regard to the allotment of time slots to the various political parties. That is why we
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion will again return to the charge, as long as the hon. Minister, who to my mind is responsible for the C.B.C. has not defined a policy in this regard.
Besides, the matter has already been cleared up by the committee, in the 1966 report concerning the White Paper on broadcasting, where the objectives of radio and television are defined. One of those objectives is to the effect that we wish to express our conviction, and another to the effect that priority of the public sector must be observed; that is one of the supreme and permanent objectives of the new act. We should develop, and not diminish, the effectiveness of the corporation, the main instrument by which our national conscience can be extended and maintained and national unity thereby strengthened.
But in the report on broadcasting, the C.B.C. is asked to promote national unity or, at least, to respect it. That is where the corporation has sinned, has erred, has taken a wrong direction, in that it allowed an hour and thirty seven minutes for the broadcasting of the program of the Ralliement Creditiste, and eight hours and forty six minutes for the broadcasting of a program opposed to national unity.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has not complied with the parliamentary committee report to this end. And the crown corporation has not been brought back to order by the responsible minister.
In the same report, it is pointed out on several occasions, that parliament has never given any guidelines to the C.B.C. with respect to the policy it should follow. But, on the other hand, when I consider the generosity with which the C.B.C. has treated the Liberal party during its convention here in Ottawa, I am amazed. I have in hand a document published by the CTV network-"The English-speaking network of the C.B.C."- about the Liberal convention held on April 4 and 5. Reference is made to the candidates to the leadership who had their publicity paid for out of public funds or moneys. The publication of that document seemed to have been costly; the president, Mr. Charles Templeton, has even his picture on page 3, where he states:

The Liberal leadership convention should be Canada's most exciting and dramatic event of the year.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the crown corporation has exceeded its right, privileges

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) cannot be here this evening, but I am sure that whichever parliamentary secretary responds to my question will convey my message to him.
On Tuesday, November 19, as recorded in Hansard at page 2912, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether he had yet set up in his department a committee or task force to study the whole question of a general application of the principle of escalat-

DEBATES	November 21, 1968
ing pensions that have been put into effect. The minister's reply was in these words:
Mr. Speaker, as indicated, I believe, earlier this session by the Prime Minister, the whole question of our various welfare programs is under review.
I went on to ask whether the specific question of escalating pensions was included in that review and the minister's reply was:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, all matters pertaining to our welfare programs are part of the review.
I suppose I should be content with that generally affirmative reply, namely that this matter in which I am deeply interested is being reviewed, but I confess to something less than complete satisfaction with that answer. As I understand it, the review the government is giving to all federal welfare programs is of the kind that considers what programs can be passed on to the provinces and what programs can be dispensed with at this time. I have seen nothing in the references to the review of welfare programs that implies any willingness to extend benefits or provisions. In fact, the classical statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was that we have had enough of this free stuff.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am not satisfied that this very serious matter should be considered as covered because there is a general review of welfare programs. The specific problem I am concerned about, and hon. members must be aware of this, is that with the speed of rising prices and costs, with the growth of affluence that is taking place, there is the danger that people on pensions will become third or fourth class citizens or that they will become people who have no chance to protect themselves against inflation or against the failure of their fixed incomes to enable them to meet the cost of living or to keep up with the rising standard of living.
I hope I have made that case clear with regard to retired civil servants, and I have tried to make it clear with regard to retired C.N.R. employees and various other workers, but it applies to everyone. It applies to people on old age security pensions and people on industrial pensions. These things are relatively recent in our way of life, considering the long haul, and I suggest that unless we look to the future and build into our program adequate provisions for escalation, our pension programs could fall apart.
Another thing that concerns me, bearing in mind that good is frequently the enemy of best, is that a pattern is being established. In a sense it is a good pattern, or I should say
November 21, 1968
that in a sense it is a good principle. I refer to the 2 per cent increase in old age security-pensions that is possible, and the same increase that is possible under the Canada Pension Plan. Two or three days ago the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) tabled the Devco report and, lo and behold, we find in there a certain pension arrangement being made for the miners of Cape Breton with a special provision being made for escalating the pensions by not more than 2 per cent per year.
I am in the position of having to welcome, and welcome wholeheartedly, this extension of the principle that pensions already in pay have to be escalated; but I am afraid that if this pattern of 2 per cent escalation, and a fixed 2 per cent, gets much wider, a good principle will be destroyed because of that kind of limitation. We can reach the situation where people's pensions will generally be increased by 2 per cent per year and they will be told that therefore they cannot expect anything more. But 2 per cent does not begin to keep up with the rising cost of living and it does not enable the sector of our society which is retired to keep up with the rising standard of living.
Therefore I am pleading for a study of the whole, broad question. I will fight it on its individual fronts, retired civil servants on pension, old age security pensioners and all the rest, but I plead that somewhere in the government-and I suggest that it be in the Department of National Health and Welfare, or perhaps the Department of Finance if the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance is going to reply-there should be established a special task force or committee to work on this problem. I suggest that it is not good enough just to have it lost somewhere in the general study of welfare programs.
The standard letter being sent out from the Prime Minister's office to people who write in regarding retired civil service pensions, and I have seen it several times, reads in this way:
The position of persons on pensions and other fixed incomes who have seen their real income diminish with the general increase in costs and prices is a matter of great concern to the government. The government, of course, cannot limit its consideration of this question to the situation of retired public servants, but must be concerned with the broader question of the problems of all pensioners and others living on limited fixed incomes.
I am not satisfied with this letter as an answer to these people, but I underline and endorse wholeheartedly the statement that comes out of the Prime Minister's office that the government must be concerned with the

WATER RESOURCES-ST. MARY'S RIVER-ACTION RESPECTING POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to

3066	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion appear on the late show this evening, with the other hon. gentlemen who are in the chamber at this time. My inquiry put to the Minister of Transport during the question period today was as follows:
In view of the report of the International Joint Commission on pollution of the St. Mary's river, does the Minister of Transport plan to take any action against the shipowners who are polluting this river by dumping waste into it?
This report which was released last week, on November 12, is a very comprehensive document which outlines the problems of pollution not only in St. Mary's river but in the St. Clair river and in the Detroit river as well. I am especially concerned with the problem of the St. Mary's river because it runs through part of my riding of Algoma. In Algoma one of our main industries is tourism, and places like St. Joseph island and Pine island which are in the flow of the St. Mary's river suffer when the waters become polluted. As a matter of fact, tourism in this area is rapidly accelerating because of an expanding urban population in Sault Ste. Marie which moves out to the rural areas every summer. However, this trend may not continue, as the pollution of the river becomes more intense. No one would want to spend a large amount of money in the purchase of a lot in this beautiful area, and go to the expense of building a summer home on it, only to find sewage, garbage and oil from lake freighters and ocean-going ships washing up on the beach.
This report of the International Joint Commission indicates that the city of Sault Ste. Marie does have an adequate sewage treatment facility and that the industries which have been putting industrial waste into the river are taking steps to correct the pollution which has been caused by them in the past. It seems to me that the Ontario water resources commission is taking positive action by building a new sewage treatment plant in Sault Ste. Marie and by encouraging the offending industries to instal anti-pollution equipment in their plants.
Now it is up to the federal government to control the ships which are dumping garbage into this river. The main problem seems to
DEBATES	November 21. 1968
occur when there is heavy traffic and the boats have to anchor in the channel, or when there is a low hanging fog over the St. Mary's river valley and ships have to anchor overnight. It is during this period of time that the bilges are pumped and sewage as well as other refuse is dumped into the river. I believe the federal government, through its inspectors in the Department of Transport, should carry on a careful surveillance of these vessels during these periods of time.
The Navigable Waters Protection Act is the statute which controls this matter. Section 20 of chapter 193, the pertinent section, reads as follows:
No person shall throw or deposit, or cause or permit to be thrown or deposited any stone, gravel, earth, cinders, ashes or other material or rubbish liable to sink to the bottom in any navigable non-tidal waters of Canada where there are not at all times at least eight fathoms of water.
It seems to me that this act gives the department the authority to stop offending ships from dumping garbage into this river. I would like to see the minister, armed with this authority, take positive steps to stop this dumping of waste into the St. Mary's river by Great Lakes freighters and by ocean going ships.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of
Transport (Mr. Hellyer) is aware of the problem outlined by the hon. member for Algoma, and I know that I speak for the minister when I say that he is greatly concerned about this matter. In the Navigable Waters Protection Act, chapter 193, sections 19 and 20, it is stated that pollution caused in the manner described by the hon. member is an offence. Enforcement of this section of the act is at the present time the responsibility of the Department of Fisheries.
It is the intention of the Minister of Transport to introduce into the house at an early date amendments to the Canada Shipping Act to correct this situation. These amendments to the act will be enforced by Department of Transport inspectors.
